title: Reconfigurable Current Distributions in Percolating Au Films and CrO2 Powder Compacts - Beyond Geometrical Connectivity
summary: Despite fundamental differences in morphology, dimensionality, and microscopic transport, semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders converge on a common network-level principle: the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network. In Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold, increasing bias reversibly shifts the low-temperature response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance, consistent with broader electronic participation of the fixed island network. In CrO2 powder compacts, magnetic field mainly changes the spin-dependent resistances of existing intergranular junctions and thereby reorders competing current paths; temperature and measuring current can additionally expand or deplete the active network. Cohn's theorem provides a compact sensitivity principle for both cases: local resistance changes influence the measured response in proportion to the current carried by the affected links. The comparison identifies two limiting but interconvertible modes of reconfiguration - link enabling and link reweighting - and shows why geometrical connectivity alone is insufficient for interpreting transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors.

AI.tldr: Semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders share a network-level principle: the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network, reconfiguring via link enabling (Au) or link reweighting (CrO2).
AI.motivation: Despite different morphology, dimensionality, and microscopic transport, the paper seeks a common network-level principle governing transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors, and to explain why geometrical connectivity alone cannot interpret their electrical response.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of two systems: semicontinuous Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold under varying bias, and compacted CrO2 powder with applied magnetic field, temperature, and measuring current. Interpretation via Cohn's theorem, which weights local resistance changes by the current carried by the affected links.
AI.result: In Au films, increasing bias reversibly shifts low-temperature response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance, reflecting broader electronic participation of the fixed island network. In CrO2 compacts, magnetic field mainly changes spin-dependent junction resistances and reorders competing current paths; temperature and measuring current expand or deplete the active network.
AI.conclusion: Two limiting but interconvertible reconfiguration modes are identified: link enabling and link reweighting. Geometrical connectivity alone is insufficient for interpreting transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors; the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network.

title: TetrisCNN for interpretable detection of phases of matter from experimental quantum simulator data
summary: Detecting phases of matter in general relies on identifying the correct order parameter - a task that remains notoriously difficult for unknown transitions and traditionally is guided by physical intuition and educated guess. Neural networks have recently offered an alternative route by locating phase transitions in known models without any a priori physical knowledge. Yet these approaches remain black boxes and only identify phases without elucidating their properties. Moreover, they often struggle when confronted with realistic, noisy experimental data, which constitute the ultimate testbed for automated methods in physics. Here, we bridge these perspectives by introducing TetrisCNN, a convolutional architecture with parallel branches of differently shaped filters, reminiscent of Tetris blocks, that learns sparse, interpretable latent representations directly in terms of spin correlators. Applied to experimental snapshots of two-dimensional Ising and XY quantum simulators measured in multiple bases, the network not only detects phase transitions and crossovers but also expresses its latent representation and decision boundaries as symbolic formulas built from experimentally measurable spin correlators. This framework opens the way to integrating interpretable neural networks with quantum simulators to uncover and understand new phases of matter.

Neural networks offer a route to locate phase transitions in known models without a priori physical knowledge, but they remain black boxes: they only identify phases without elucidating their properties and often struggle with realistic, noisy experimental data—the ultimate testbed for automated methods in physics.

This design learns sparse, interpretable latent representations directly in terms of spin correlators. title: Qupertino: Pure MLX Array Kernels versus Hand-Tuned Metal Shaders for Quantum Circuit Simulation on Apple Silicon
summary: We present Qupertino, an open-source quantum circuit simulator for Apple Silicon, and use it to ask how far a simulator written purely in MLX array operations can go and what remains for hand-tuned Metal shaders. The framework ships two measured tiers. The pure tier dispatches structured gates to specialized MLX kernels: diagonal gates run as broadcast phase multiplies, controlled gates as masked half-state updates, and SWAP as an axis permutation; a paired dense-path ablation attributes a 25-33x speedup to this dispatch alone. The opt-in shader tier adds hand-written Metal kernels for every structured layer family in our benchmarks, including phase-LUT diagonals, GF(2) affine permutation gathers, fused tensor-product single-qubit layers, radix-4 QFT and Walsh-Hadamard butterflies, and basis-conjugated XX/YY Trotter layers; runtime fusion detectors route work to them while preserving circuit semantics exactly, confirmed by parity tests. In a four-way interleaved campaign on M1 Max (two warmups, ten measured repeats per cell), the shader tier is fastest by mean runtime in all 18 comparison cells against same-machine Qiskit Aer CPU and PennyLane lightning.qubit. At 25 qubits, gate-stream QFT runs in 0.0591 +/- 0.0029 s (paired 47.2x over Aer, 95.3x over PennyLane) and TFIM Trotter evolution in 0.495 +/- 0.035 s (36.2x and 67.2x). Across a 29-workload suite, the shader tier's paired speedup over pure MLX reaches 25x, with 25 of 29 workloads accelerating above parity. The framework also supports variational ansatz workloads, QAOA, QCBM, Trotter-Suzuki Hamiltonian simulation, and OpenQASM 2.0 import (unitary subset); a preliminary MPS backend reaches 150 qubits on limited-entanglement workloads. Correctness rests on 253 Python tests, independent complex128 checks, and a Trotter-error curve against exact diagonalization. State-vector memory remains exponential in qubit count.

title: AlchemQ: Proof-Carrying Quantum Circuit Optimization with Per-Result Equivalence Certificates
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Pilot run on IBM Heron r2. Certificate spec, reference verifier, benchmark and certificate corpora, raw hardware data: https://github.com/a1damek1125/AlchemQ (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0), archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX . Engine proprietary; certificates verifiable without it. LLM-assisted drafting; see Acknowledgments
summary: We present AlchemQ v0.5, a proof-of-concept system that couples an untrusted beam-search optimizer with a machine-checkable per-result certification layer and a versioned certificate protocol (0.2.0), so that every optimized circuit ships with a verifiable artifact rather than a bare claim. The certifier proves equivalence up to global phase by ZX-calculus full reduction, with a numeric-tensor fallback based on the optimal Hilbert-Schmidt overlap. Certificates are self-contained and tamper-evident: canonical gate-canon-v1 hashes, measured residuals, tri-state verdicts (certified/rejected/inconclusive), and versioned phase-note schemas for cross-platform reproducibility. The agent aggregates three fuzzy t-norms, cannot return an uncertified circuit, and since v0.4 guarantees no componentwise regression against the original. On a benchmark of 100 circuits, all 400 optimizations terminate without error, every returned circuit is certified, every mutation is detected, and a 2998-test suite passes on two platforms. The PyZX baseline is strong (21.4% mean T-count reduction over 82 circuits) and the agent is strictly better on 9/100; the three t-norms return identical circuits on all 100 standard instances, diverging only on 4/38 of an adversarial suite. Two case studies are new: a false negative root-caused to a pivot-normalization bug in PyZX's compare_tensors (pivot 4.7e-9; the optimal-overlap residual is 7.4e-11), and eight certificates rejected on macOS due to BLAS-dependent floats in phase_note. Both were fixed; all artifact sets validate 400/400 on both platforms. A pilot run on IBM Heron r2 gives a certified circuit 78% shallower with 65% fewer two-qubit gates; output quality favors it on all three metrics but is not significant at 1024 shots. We release the certificate specification and a standalone reference verifier (Apache-2.0) with data and scripts; the engine is proprietary.

title: Femtoscopic Correlation Functions in Density Operator Representation
summary: Femtoscopic correlation functions (CFs) have been increasingly used to extract strong interactions between pairs of unstable particles, but their physical soundness has recently been questioned. To answer this, we formulate CFs at the operator level, with the observed subsystem described by a reduced density operator and subsequent dynamics absorbed into an effective measurement operator. The Koonin-Pratt form is recovered under four well-motivated reductions. The formulation makes explicit that the source-side and interaction-side representations must be consistently matched, and motivates an operational convention in which a measured reference correlation establishes a compatible source--interaction pairing that can be extended to other pairs for CF-to-CF predictions.

title: Holomorphic Quantum Error Correction Codes
summary: We develop a holomorphic representation of quantum error correction codes (QECCs) within the Segal--Bargmann space. By encoding qubits into Schwinger boson modes $(z_{a_j}, z_{b_j})$ subject to a degree-one homogeneity constraint, we derive closed-form differential operator representations for stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery for fundamental codes (three-, five-, seven-, and nine-qubit codes). Quantum errors are characterized as holomorphic perturbations violating this constraint, while syndrome measurement projects onto eigenspaces of commuting differential operators. Restricting to unit-magnitude variables ($|z|=1$) reveals a toroidal space $\T^{2n}$ where error syndromes manifest as discrete translations in winding number space $\Z^{2n}$, and recovery acts as Hamiltonian flows restoring the winding configuration. In the full Segal--Bargmann space, the code space is a holomorphic submanifold of $\CP^{2^n-1}$, with correctable errors as transverse normal directions. Consequently, the Knill--Laflamme condition becomes a Fubini--Study orthogonality condition between the code submanifold and its error-translated images. Topological protection emerges from the $U(1)^n$ fiber bundle structure: global phase noise along fibers is unobservable, while base-space errors require active correction. Finally, we establish a path-integral formulation for semiclassical error correction dynamics and show that geometric entanglement via the Segre embedding naturally quantifies code distance. This framework unifies algebraic, geometric, and topological perspectives on fault-tolerant quantum protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a holomorphic representation of quantum error correction codes in the Segal-Bargmann space, unifying algebraic, geometric, and topological perspectives on fault-tolerant quantum protocols.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified framework for quantum error correction by reformulating stabilizers, syndromes, recovery, and the Knill-Laflamme condition in geometric and topological terms.
AI.method: Qubits are encoded into Schwinger boson modes with a degree-one homogeneity constraint. Closed-form differential operators represent stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery for the three-, five-, seven-, and nine-qubit codes. Errors are modeled as holomorphic perturbations, syndrome measurement as projection onto eigenspaces of commuting differential operators, and recovery as Hamiltonian flows on a toroidal space. The code space is described as a holomorphic submanifold of CP^{2^n-1}, and a path-integral formulation addresses semiclassical dynamics.
AI.result: Restricting to |z|=1 yields a torus T^{2n} where syndromes become discrete translations in winding-number space Z^{2n} and recovery restores the winding configuration. The Knill-Laflamme condition becomes a Fubini-Study orthogonality condition between the code submanifold and its error-translated images. Topological protection arises from a U(1)^n fiber bundle structure, with fiber phase noise unobservable and base-space errors requiring active correction. Geometric entanglement via the Segre embedding quantifies code distance.
AI.conclusion: The Segal-Bargmann holomorphic representation unifies algebraic, geometric, and topological views of quantum error correction, offering a coherent framework for fault-tolerant quantum protocols.

title: Energy-Constrained Commutator Variance for Weyl Pairs
summary: Let $W$ be a representation of the Weyl relations on a separable Hilbert space and write $\mathcal R_W(K)=\{W(f):f\in K\}''$. If the symplectic pairing of $K_1$ and $K_2$ is nonzero, there is a self-adjoint unitary $B\in\mathcal R_W(K_2)$ such that, for every normal state $ρ$, one can choose a self-adjoint unitary $A_ρ\in\mathcal R_W(K_1)$ with $\operatorname{Var}_ρ(-i[A_ρ,B])=4$. Hence the optimized mean-input-energy-constrained coefficient equals $4$ at every admissible energy threshold. For the fixed trigonometric Weyl witness $h$, an exact identity for $4-h^2$ reduces the deficit to a phase-fixed problem for commuting squared Weyl translations. For the one-mode quadratic energy $G_M=\frac12 R^TMR-\frac12\sqrt{\det M}$, with $M>0$ and $u^TΩv=π$, we prove $4-γ_{G_M,E}(h)=\frac{u^TMu+v^TMv+2π\sqrt{\det M}}{4E}+O(E^{-2})$. The lower bound holds over all normal states satisfying the mean-energy constraint, and a localized Zak construction attains the same coefficient. For $G=dΓ(H_1)$ and witness directions $u,v\in\operatorname{dom}H_1^{1/2}$, the fixed-witness deficit is $Θ(E^{-1})$ whenever at least one direction lies outside $\ker H_1$; if both directions are zero modes, the constrained supremum equals the endpoint at every positive threshold.

AI.tldr: The paper studies state-independent energy-constrained uncertainty relations for Weyl algebras, showing an exact coefficient of 4 from symplectic pairing, deriving an asymptotic expansion 4−γ_{G_M,E}(h) = (u^TMu+v^TMv+2π√det M)/(4E)+O(E^{-2}) for one-mode quadratic energies, and establishing Θ(E^{-1}) behavior for general quadratic generators.
AI.motivation: Quantify how much two Weyl-subalgebra observables can be jointly "non-commuting" (variance of their commutator) under a mean-energy constraint when the symplectic pairing of the underlying directions is nonzero, and turn this into a computable, state-independent coefficient for realistic quadratic energy observables.
AI.method: Use the Weyl relations on a separable Hilbert space and von Neumann algebras R_W(K) generated by Weyl unitaries over symplectic subspaces. For nonzero symplectic pairing, construct a self-adjoint unitary B in R_W(K_2) such that for every normal state one can find a self-adjoint unitary A_ρ in R_W(K_1) with Var_ρ(−i[A_ρ,B])=4. Reduce the deficit 4−h^2 to a phase-fixed problem for commuting squared Weyl translations (trigonometric Weyl witness). For the one-mode quadratic energy G_M, use M>0, u^TΩv=π and asymptotic analysis in E; construct a lower bound over all normal states with a mean-energy constraint and match it with a localized Zak construction.
AI.result: The optimized mean-input-energy-constrained coefficient equals 4 at every admissible energy threshold. For the fixed trigonometric Weyl witness h, an exact identity for 4−h^2 reduces the deficit to a phase-fixed problem for commuting squared Weyl translations. For G_M=½R^TMR−½√det M with M>0 and u^TΩv=π, it holds that 4−γ_{G_M,E}(h)=(u^TMu+v^TMv+2π√det M)/(4E)+O(E^{-2}); the lower bound holds over all normal states satisfying the mean-energy constraint and a localized Zak construction attains the same coefficient. For G=dΓ(H_1) with u,v in dom H_1^{1/2}, the fixed-witness deficit is Θ(E^{-1}) whenever at least one direction lies outside ker H_1; if both directions are zero modes, the constrained supremum equals the endpoint at every positive threshold.
AI.conclusion: State-independent commutator-variance bounds for Weyl observables are governed by the symplectic pairing and saturate at the value 4. For quadratic energies the sharp energy-constrained deficit is asymptotically determined by a symplectic-covariant expression (u^TMu+v^TMv+2π√det M)/(4E), with matching lower and upper bounds; the general quadratic-generator case yields Θ(E^{-1}) deficits except in degenerate zero-mode directions where the constrained supremum is exactly the endpoint.

title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
comment: 32 + 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; topical review, comments welcome!
summary: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.

AI.tldr: A hands-on review of Trotter decompositions and related product/splitting formulae for time evolution, covering recent algorithmic advances, improved error bounds, noisy quantum hardware applications, and generalisations/alternatives to Trotterization.
AI.motivation: Trotter decompositions, splitting methods and Lie product formulae are ubiquitous for simulating time evolution across classical and quantum computing, yet the field has advanced substantially over the last decade in algorithm design, error analysis, and quantum-hardware relevance. A consolidated, practically oriented overview is needed.
AI.method: A theoretical-physicist-perspective review that surveys state-of-the-art time evolution algorithms, emphasises recently discovered efficient schemes and their practical use, presents improved error bound estimation, discusses relevance to noisy quantum hardware, and gives a comprehensive overview of generalisations and alternatives. Mathematical proofs and technical details are omitted for readability.
AI.result: The review identifies recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms, explains how to use them in practice, documents greatly improved error bounds from the past decade, and provides a comprehensive map of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization, including time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, and Crouch-Grossman methods.
AI.conclusion: The work serves as a hands-on guide and a reference starting point, reframing Trotter-type methods as a coherent, evolving toolkit spanning classical and quantum applications, with practical guidance and pointers for further detail.

title: Enhanced Emission and Two-Photon Interference of Lead-Vacancy Centers in Diamond Solid Immersion Lenses
summary: A negatively charged lead-vacancy (PbV-) center in diamond is a novel quantum system which can be operated at a high temperature above 4 K owing to its large ground state splitting. To unlock the quantum properties of the PbV- center, the enhancement of the fluorescence intensity is a key issue. Here, we demonstrate enhanced emission from PbV- centers by a factor of approximately 10 using solid immersion lenses (SILs) fabricated on rough diamond surface caused by high-temperature anneal over 2000°C. Resonant excitation reveals the narrow emission close to the transform-limited linewidth. Furthermore, we demonstrate two-photon interference using one single PbV- center in an SIL. This enhanced emission and indistinguishability will lead to further development of the PbV- center towards quantum network node applications.

AI.tldr: Enhanced emission from negatively charged lead-vacancy (PbV-) centers in diamond by ~10× using solid immersion lenses (SILs) on rough annealed diamond surfaces, with near-transform-limited linewidth and two-photon interference from a single center, enabling quantum network node applications.
AI.motivation: The PbV- center in diamond is a promising high-temperature (>4 K) quantum system due to its large ground state splitting, but its weak fluorescence intensity limits exploration and exploitation of its quantum properties, so emission enhancement is a key prerequisite.
AI.method: Solid immersion lenses (SILs) were fabricated on diamond surfaces that were deliberately made rough by high-temperature annealing above 2000°C. Resonant excitation spectroscopy characterized the emission linewidth, and two-photon interference measurements were performed on a single PbV- center inside an SIL.
AI.result: Emission from PbV- centers was enhanced by approximately a factor of 10. Resonant excitation revealed narrow emission approaching the transform-limited linewidth, and two-photon interference was successfully demonstrated using one single PbV- center in an SIL.
AI.conclusion: The combination of enhanced emission and high indistinguishability positions the PbV- center as a viable building block for quantum network node applications, motivating further development.

title: Lazy training of quantum physics informed neural networks
summary: We study the gradient-flow training dynamics of quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) for the solution of second-order elliptic partial differential equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We consider parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators and analyze their overparameterized regime through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). Our contribution is a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for QPINNs and their variational formulation: we prove that, for sufficiently large circuit width, the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model, with explicit bounds depending on the number of qubits, circuit depth, circuit light-cone geometry, and the dimension of the domain of the solution to the PDE.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for overparameterized quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) applied to second-order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions, proving that gradient-flow training is well-approximated by a linearized neural tangent kernel (NTK) model when circuit width is sufficiently large.
AI.motivation: QPINNs combine parameterized quantum circuits with physics-informed learning for solving PDEs, but their gradient-flow training dynamics remain theoretically poorly understood. The paper aims to characterize when and how the nonlinear training of QPINNs can be reliably reduced to a tractable linearized description.
AI.method: The authors model function approximators as parameterized quantum circuits and analyze the overparameterized regime via the neural tangent kernel (NTK). They establish a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for QPINNs and their variational formulation, deriving explicit error bounds that depend on the number of qubits, circuit depth, circuit light-cone geometry, and the dimension of the PDE solution domain.
AI.result: For sufficiently large circuit width, the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model, with explicit nonasymptotic bounds tying approximation quality to qubit count, circuit depth, light-cone geometry, and spatial dimension.
AI.conclusion: QPINNs in the overparameterized regime admit a rigorous lazy-training characterization, justifying the use of linearized NTK dynamics for analyzing and understanding their gradient-flow training for second-order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions.

title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
comment: 15 pages in the main text (5 figures, 1 table); 104 pages total (5 figures, 10 tables)
summary: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding $k\geq3$ logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable $S$ and $\mathrm{CX}$ gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires $n=Θ(2^k)$ physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by $S$ and $\mathrm{CZ}$, require only $n=Θ(k^2)$ physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and $\mathrm{CX}$-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general theory of automorphism gates for stabilizer codes, showing the largest logical group for k≥3 qubits is generated by addressable S and CX gates (at cost n=Θ(2^k)), while addressable diagonal Clifford gates need only n=Θ(k^2), revealing that the key qubit-cost divide is between diagonal and CX-type gates rather than Clifford and non-Clifford.
AI.motivation: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing relies on combining cheap specialized operations with expensive versatile ones. Automorphism gates are cheap (physical single-qubit Cliffords plus qubit permutations), but no general theory characterized their maximum logical power or the minimum code size required to achieve it.

They characterize the largest logical group generated by addressable S and CX gates, construct codes attaining it, and classify the largest logical groups achievable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, with refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. They then derive tight physical-qubit-cost bounds, extending the analysis to addressable diagonal gates at any fixed Clifford hierarchy level.

Achieving the maximum-size logical group via automorphisms requires n=Θ(2^k) physical qubits, whereas all addressable diagonal Clifford gates (generated by S and CZ) require only n=Θ(k^2) using physical single-qubit Cliffords. Both bounds are tight.
AI.conclusion: The polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed Clifford hierarchy level. Consequently, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and CX-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

title: Theory of post-selected entanglement transitions in monitored bosons
summary: Entanglement phase transitions driven by quantum measurements have emerged as a central paradigm in open quantum many-body physics. Such phase transitions are well established for systems with finite local Hilbert-space dimensions, such as qubits and fermions, while their realization in bosonic systems with unbounded local occupation numbers remains poorly understood. Even in the absence of interactions, number states of bosons are intrinsically non-Gaussian, preventing the use of standard correlation-matrix approaches. To address this problem, we develop a replica-free Keldysh field-theoretic framework that expresses the Renyi entropy of bosonic systems initialized in on-site Fock states in terms of permanents of matrices constructed from single-particle Green's functions. Applying this framework to a continuously monitored one-dimensional cross-stitch lattice conditioned on the no-click trajectory, we uncover a transition from volume-law to logarithmic entanglement scaling. We show that the transition is controlled by a restructuring of the non-Hermitian spectrum that changes the number of long-lived modes from extensive to finite. In the strongly monitored regime, bosons dynamically condense into a microscopic number of slowest-decaying modes, producing logarithmic entanglement scaling, whereas an extensive manifold of long-lived modes at weak monitoring gives rise to volume-law entanglement. Our results establish a distinct mechanism for measurement-induced entanglement transitions in free bosonic systems and provide a computationally efficient diagnostic of the measurement-induced bosonic condensation.

AI.motivation: Entanglement phase transitions driven by quantum measurements are well established for finite local Hilbert-space dimensions (qubits, fermions), but their realization in bosonic systems with unbounded occupation numbers remains poorly understood. Standard correlation-matrix approaches fail because bosonic number states are intrinsically non-Gaussian even without interactions.
AI.method: The authors develop a replica-free Keldysh field-theoretic framework that expresses the Renyi entropy of bosonic systems initialized in on-site Fock states in terms of permanents of matrices built from single-particle Green's functions. They apply it to a continuously monitored one-dimensional cross-stitch lattice conditioned on the no-click trajectory.

The transition is controlled by a restructuring of the non-Hermitian spectrum changing the number of long-lived modes from extensive to finite. Strong monitoring causes bosons to condense into a microscopic number of slowest-decaying modes giving logarithmic scaling, while an extensive manifold of long-lived modes at weak monitoring yields volume-law entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a distinct mechanism for measurement-induced entanglement transitions in free bosonic systems and provide a computationally efficient diagnostic of measurement-induced bosonic condensation.

title: Emergent classicality and wavefunction branching in an isolated quantum many-body system
summary: Decoherence in quantum systems is conventionally modeled as the effect of interactions with an external environment. However, such a prescription excludes isolated many-body systems, which are also expected to display classical behavior at macroscopic scales. In isolated systems, decoherence must emerge internally from microscopic degrees of freedom that are invisible to the macroscopic description. Here we explicitly show that classicality can emerge in such a fashion. We consider a weakly disordered, $3$-local chaotic kicked top of $N$ qubits, where the collective spin sector serves as the macroscopic description, while the microscopic permutation sector acts as an internal bath, decohering the collective spin sector. Starting from closed unitary dynamics, we derive and numerically confirm an effective Lindblad equation for the collective spin variables. In the thermodynamic limit these reduced dynamics converge to a classical chaotic Fokker--Planck equation with vanishingly small diffusion on the spherical phase space, producing a quantum-classical correspondence beyond the Ehrenfest time. The chaotic dynamics evolve the pure many-body wavefunction into continuously branching components associated with distinct classical trajectories. These branches acquire nearly orthogonal microscopic records in the permutation sector, preventing quantum interferences and ensuring the corresponding histories remain consistent.

AI.tldr: Classicality can emerge internally in isolated many-body systems, without an external environment. In a weakly disordered 3-local chaotic kicked top of N qubits, the permutation (microscopic) sector acts as an internal bath that decoheres the collective spin (macroscopic) sector, yielding an effective Lindblad equation and, in the thermodynamic limit, a classical chaotic Fokker–Planck equation.
AI.motivation: Standard decoherence models require an external environment, which excludes isolated many-body systems. Yet isolated systems are also expected to show classical behavior at macroscopic scales, so decoherence must arise internally from microscopic degrees of freedom hidden from the macroscopic description. The paper aims to demonstrate such emergent classicality explicitly.
AI.method: A weakly disordered, 3-local chaotic kicked top of N qubits is studied. The collective spin sector is treated as the macroscopic description, and the microscopic permutation sector as an internal bath. Starting from closed unitary dynamics, an effective Lindblad master equation for the collective spin variables is derived and numerically confirmed.
AI.result: The reduced collective-spin dynamics converge, in the thermodynamic limit, to a classical chaotic Fokker–Planck equation with vanishingly small diffusion on the spherical phase space. This yields a quantum–classical correspondence valid beyond the Ehrenfest time. The chaotic evolution drives the pure many-body wavefunction into continuously branching components tied to distinct classical trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Internal decoherence from microscopic permutation degrees of freedom suffices to produce classicality in isolated systems. The branching components acquire nearly orthogonal microscopic records in the permutation sector, which suppress quantum interference and keep the corresponding histories consistent—an internally generated mechanism for the emergence of classical behavior.

title: A Square-Root Barrier to Quantum Gate Speed under Linear Coupling
summary: Faster quantum gates can suppress the decoherence accumulated during a computation, but in superconducting processors stronger microwave pulses can also increase leakage, off-resonant excitation, stray-field errors, and crosstalk. This creates a central energy--speed--error tradeoff: can quantum state engineering make a gate parametrically faster without paying proportionally more drive energy? We address this question by treating the driving pulse as a quantum bosonic field rather than a classical waveform. For a finite-dimensional system coupled linearly to that field, we prove that fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of the pulse energy, under stated uniformity conditions on the coupling and accepted dynamics. The bound permits arbitrary pulse states, including squeezed and non-Gaussian states, as well as drive--system entanglement and back action; coherent Gaussian pulses attain its energy exponent. Thus squeezing or other state engineering alone cannot replace the square-root energy law of a conventional linear drive by the linear scaling allowed by general quantum speed limits. Achieving that improvement requires changing the interaction class, in addition to using a suitable nonclassical pulse, thereby identifying interaction nonlinearity as an essential resource for relaxing the practical gate-speed error tradeoff.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for a finite-dimensional system linearly coupled to a quantum bosonic driving field, fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of pulse energy under uniformity conditions, so state engineering (e.g., squeezing) cannot beat the square-root energy law of conventional linear drives.
AI.motivation: Faster quantum gates reduce decoherence, but stronger microwave pulses in superconducting processors worsen leakage, off-resonant excitation, stray-field errors, and crosstalk. This creates an energy–speed–error tradeoff, raising the question of whether quantum state engineering can make a gate parametrically faster without proportionally more drive energy.
AI.method: The driving pulse is treated as a quantum bosonic field rather than a classical waveform. For a finite-dimensional system linearly coupled to that field, the authors prove a bound on fixed-fidelity gate transition rates as a function of pulse energy, under stated uniformity conditions on the coupling and accepted dynamics, allowing arbitrary pulse states (including squeezed and non-Gaussian states) and drive–system entanglement with back action.
AI.result: Fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of the pulse energy. Coherent Gaussian pulses attain this energy exponent, showing the bound is tight within the linear-coupling class.
AI.conclusion: Squeezing or other state engineering alone cannot replace the square-root energy law of a conventional linear drive with the linear scaling permitted by general quantum speed limits. Achieving such improvement requires changing the interaction class, identifying interaction nonlinearity as an essential resource for relaxing the practical gate-speed–error tradeoff.

title: Temporal information processing on a 4,500-qubit quantum annealer
summary: Quantum machine learning could uncover statistical structure beyond the reach of classical models, but this requires quantum models large and expressive enough to be useful and cheap enough to read out. Most approaches optimize many quantum parameters and are thus limited by expensive training loops. Here we report a quantum machine-learning model implemented on a programmable superconducting quantum annealer that processes temporal data at large scale using up to 4,500 qubits-the largest quantum machine-learning experiment performed to date. Following the quantum reservoir computing paradigm, the untrained native many-body dynamics generated by reverse annealing is directly used to process temporal data. We prove that the interactions produced during annealing are indispensable-a non-interacting reservoir retains no memory of its input. We evaluate our model experimentally on standard memory benchmarks and demonstrate that it can successfully forecast chaotic time series. These results establish quantum annealers as a scalable platform for large-scale quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: This work implements a quantum reservoir computing model on a programmable superconducting quantum annealer, using native untrained many-body dynamics from reverse annealing to process temporal data with up to 4,500 qubits—the largest quantum ML experiment to date. The authors prove interactions during annealing are essential for memory, and demonstrate practical performance on memory benchmarks and chaotic time-series forecasting.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning promises to capture statistical structure beyond classical models, but this requires quantum models that are both large and expressive yet cheap to read out. Most existing approaches optimize many quantum parameters, which is bottlenecked by expensive training loops. The authors seek a scalable paradigm that avoids costly parameter optimization while exploiting large-scale quantum dynamics.
AI.method: The authors adopt the quantum reservoir computing paradigm, in which untrained native many-body dynamics generated by reverse annealing in a programmable superconducting quantum annealer directly process temporal data, leaving the reservoir fixed and only a simple readout to be trained. They scale the system up to 4,500 qubits and provide a theoretical proof that the interactions produced during annealing are indispensable: a non-interacting reservoir retains no memory of its input. They then evaluate the model experimentally on standard memory benchmarks and on chaotic time-series forecasting.
AI.result: The model was successfully implemented at large scale on up to 4,500 qubits, constituting the largest quantum machine-learning experiment performed to date. It performed well on standard memory benchmarks and successfully forecast chaotic time series. The theoretical analysis confirmed that interaction-driven many-body dynamics are required for memory, as a non-interacting reservoir retains no input memory.
AI.conclusion: By using untrained native many-body dynamics from reverse annealing for temporal processing, this work establishes quantum annealers as a scalable platform for large-scale quantum machine learning, avoiding expensive parameter-training loops while achieving state-of-the-art scale and demonstrating practical temporal-data capabilities.

title: Quantum tree networks: complete semidefinite hierarchies and the source-transfer model
summary: Understanding the capabilities and limits of quantum systems is central to quantum information processing. This includes determining which correlations can arise in networks of quantum systems distributed by independent sources. Yet for general quantum networks, no systematic, dimension-free method is known to bound these correlations arbitrarily well. We resolve this problem for all quantum tree networks through a new source-transfer model, which we prove equivalent to a mixed quantum model. The mixed model places no restriction on dimension and reduces to the standard tensor-product model in finite dimensions; the source-transfer model instead describes these correlations through states on $C^*$-algebras and completely positive maps composed recursively along the tree. We prove the equivalence by reconstructing local measurements as Radon-Nikodym derivatives in the spatial tensor products prescribed by the network. Building on this characterization, we establish two convergent outer hierarchies of semidefinite programs (SDPs): a novel source-transfer hierarchy and the inflation-NPA hierarchy. For the source-transfer hierarchy, we extend noncommutative real algebraic geometry to multi-state polynomials with completely positive maps, prove a reconstruction theorem establishing its convergence, and give a sufficient stopping criterion for extracting finite-dimensional realizations. For the inflation-NPA hierarchy, we reconstruct source-transfer realizations from weak-operator limits of averages over source copies. Consequently, the game-value promise problem for quantum tree networks in the mixed model is $\mathsf{coRE}$-complete.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the problem of bounding correlations in general quantum tree networks by introducing a source-transfer model proven equivalent to an unbounded-dimension mixed quantum model, and establishes two convergent SDP outer hierarchies for computing these correlations.
AI.motivation: Understanding the capabilities and limits of quantum systems is central to quantum information processing, including determining which correlations can arise in networks of quantum systems distributed by independent sources. For general quantum networks, no systematic, dimension-free method was known to bound these correlations arbitrarily well.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new source-transfer model, describing correlations via states on C*-algebras and completely positive maps composed recursively along the tree, and prove it equivalent to a mixed quantum model that places no dimension restriction and reduces to the standard tensor-product model in finite dimensions. Equivalence is proven by reconstructing local measurements as Radon-Nikodym derivatives in the spatial tensor products prescribed by the network. They also extend noncommutative real algebraic geometry to multi-state polynomials with completely positive maps.
AI.result: Two convergent outer hierarchies of semidefinite programs (SDPs) are established: a novel source-transfer hierarchy (with a reconstruction theorem proving convergence and a sufficient stopping criterion for extracting finite-dimensional realizations) and the inflation-NPA hierarchy (with source-transfer realizations reconstructed from weak-operator limits of averages over source copies). Consequently, the game-value promise problem for quantum tree networks in the mixed model is shown to be coRE-complete.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic, dimension-free characterization of correlations in all quantum tree networks, along with convergent SDP hierarchies for bounding them arbitrarily well, and establishes the coRE-completeness of the game-value promise problem in the mixed model.

title: Observing and evading quantum back-action on a kilogram-scale oscillator
comment: Main text 8 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary 10 pages, 7 figures
summary: Continuous quantum displacement measurements are fundamentally limited by a trade-off between readout imprecision and measurement back-action, constrained by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In the Laser Interferometric Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), these two quantum noise components dominate much of the observation band, making it an excellent testbed. We induce a sub-Hz-linewidth optomechanical mode by trapping the differential motion of the 40-kg mirrors in a band where radiation-pressure back-action dominates the motion. Engineering the quantum state entering the dark port creates correlations between imprecision and back-action that partially cancel their contributions, reducing observed motion near resonance by ~47%. A framework resolving the imprecision, back-action, and correlation terms identifies the origin of this suppression. These results demonstrate quantum back-action evasion and quantum reservoir engineering in a macroscopic optomechanical system.

AI.tldr: Continuous displacement measurements are limited by the imprecision–back-action trade-off from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Using LIGO's 40-kg mirrors, the authors create a sub-Hz-linewidth optomechanical mode and engineer the dark-port quantum state to introduce correlations that partially cancel imprecision and back-action, suppressing observed motion near resonance by ~47%, demonstrating quantum back-action evasion and reservoir engineering in a macroscopic system.
AI.motivation: Continuous quantum displacement measurements face an intrinsic trade-off between readout imprecision and measurement back-action, bounded by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In LIGO these two quantum noise components dominate much of the observation band, making it an ideal platform to test strategies that circumvent this limit.
AI.method: The differential motion of the 40-kg LIGO mirrors is trapped to induce a sub-Hz-linewidth optomechanical mode in a band where radiation-pressure back-action dominates. The quantum state entering the dark port is engineered to create correlations between imprecision and back-action noise, and a framework is used to resolve the imprecision, back-action, and correlation contributions.
AI.result: The engineered correlations partially cancel imprecision and back-action contributions, reducing the observed motion near resonance by ~47%. The decomposition framework identifies the origin of this suppression.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates quantum back-action evasion and quantum reservoir engineering in a macroscopic optomechanical system, showing that the imprecision–back-action trade-off can be partially circumvented in LIGO-scale detectors.

title: Transformers as Intrinsic Optimizers for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading variational framework for combinatorial optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware, but its practical performance depends strongly on the classical optimizer used to train its variational parameters. This outer-loop optimization is often nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and costly when repeated across large families of related problem instances. In this work, we propose a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, in which the optimizer itself is learned and embedded directly into the hybrid quantum-classical loop. The proposed graph-conditioned Transformer processes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, thereby reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. We develop a mathematical formulation of this intrinsic-optimization perspective and evaluate the method on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings, with comparisons against representative classical and learned optimization baselines. The results demonstrate that Transformer-based intrinsic optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, embedding a learned graph-conditioned optimizer directly into the quantum-classical loop to amortize parameter training as a learned policy, and evaluates it on MaxCut benchmarks.
AI.motivation: QAOA's practical performance depends heavily on the classical optimizer used for its variational parameters. This outer-loop optimization is nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and expensive when repeated across many related instances, motivating a learned, transferable optimization mechanism.
AI.method: A graph-conditioned Transformer processes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. A mathematical formulation of the intrinsic-optimization perspective is developed.
AI.result: Evaluated on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings and compared against representative classical and learned optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based intrinsic optimization provides a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms.

title: Fifty Years of the GKLS Master Equation: Foundations and Early Developments
comment: To be published in the special volume of OSID dedicated to the 50th anniversary of the GKLS master equation
summary: The year 2026 marks the fiftieth anniversary of the two seminal papers in which Gorini, Kossakowski, and Sudarshan, and independently Lindblad, characterized the generators of completely positive quantum dynamical semigroups. We revisit the conceptual and historical route leading to the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) master equation and examine several of its early developments and consequences. Our aim is to show how several initially separate mathematical and physical ideas converged in the GKLS structure theorem, imme- diately opening the way to manifold consequences for the description of dissipative quantum phenomena and how that theorem, fifty years later, remains both a foundational result and an active framework for open quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: A historical and conceptual review of the GKLS master equation on its fiftieth anniversary, tracing how separate mathematical and physical ideas converged into the GKLS structure theorem and reviewing its early developments.
AI.motivation: The year 2026 marks the 50th anniversary of the independent papers by Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan and Lindblad characterizing generators of completely positive quantum dynamical semigroups. The authors aim to revisit the conceptual and historical route leading to the GKLS master equation and reassess its lasting significance.
AI.method: Historical and conceptual analysis: the authors trace the separate mathematical and physical ideas that converged in the GKLS structure theorem, and examine several of its early developments and consequences.
AI.result: The initially separate mathematical and physical strands are shown to converge in the GKLS structure theorem, which immediately opened the way to manifold consequences for describing dissipative quantum phenomena.
AI.conclusion: Fifty years later, the GKLS theorem remains both a foundational result and an active framework for open quantum dynamics.

title: Scalable Simulation of Quantum Dynamics on Topological Quantum Hardware
summary: Quantum computers offer a significant advantage in simulating quantum systems compared to classical computers for certain problems, although most current applications are limited to calculating static molecular properties using hybrid quantum-classical hardware. In this work, we establish a framework for the representation of quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems, designed for execution on topological quantum hardware. By leveraging the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, we utilize the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a range of systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms across a hierarchy of complexity, from two-level systems and one dimensional double-well potentials to condensed phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics. These algorithms provide a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for simulating quantum molecular dynamics on topological quantum hardware using non-Abelian anyon braiding and the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm, demonstrating it across problems of increasing complexity.
AI.motivation: Most current quantum computing applications focus on static molecular properties via hybrid quantum-classical hardware, leaving quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems underexplored. A robust, scalable framework is needed for simulating such dynamics on fault-tolerant hardware.
AI.method: The authors leverage the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons and apply the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a range of physical systems.
AI.result: The algorithms were validated across a hierarchy of complexity: two-level systems, one-dimensional double-well potentials, condensed-phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithms offer a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed-phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
title: Efficiently estimating failure rates of fault-tolerant logical non-Clifford blocks
summary: Useful quantum computation requires the fault-tolerant implementations of a universal gate set which are generically not efficiently simulable. We devise an algebraic framework that allows for efficient sampling from the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits that implement diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy. Upon successful sampling we also provide sufficient conditions for decoding success. The resulting estimate for the logical failure rate is an overestimate, which becomes more accurate for blocks that are fault tolerant against arbitrary local errors. The non-Clifford simulation overhead is independent of the number of logical qubits, making the method particularly attractive for large-scale simulations. The framework is based on viewing the non-Clifford gates in the circuit as a cohomology invariant of an underlying spacetime fault complex. The method can also be interfaced with Clifford simulators to simulate larger fault-tolerant circuits and algorithmic subroutines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an algebraic framework for efficiently sampling the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits implementing diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, with bounded non-Clifford simulation overhead independent of the logical qubit count.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant implementation of a universal gate set is required for useful quantum computation, but universal gate sets are generically not efficiently simulable. Simulating the non-Clifford (magic) resources of fault-tolerant circuits is the main bottleneck, and existing methods scale poorly with the number of logical qubits, limiting their use for large-scale simulations.
AI.method: An algebraic framework that treats non-Clifford gates in the circuit as a cohomology invariant of an underlying spacetime fault complex. This enables efficient sampling from the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits implementing diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, and provides sufficient conditions for decoding success upon successful sampling. The method can be interfaced with Clifford simulators to handle larger fault-tolerant circuits and algorithmic subroutines.
AI.result: Efficient sampling of the measurement distribution is achieved for the targeted circuits, together with sufficient conditions for decoding success. The resulting estimate of the logical failure rate is an overestimate, becoming more accurate for blocks that are fault tolerant against arbitrary local errors. The non-Clifford simulation overhead is independent of the number of logical qubits.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an efficient, scalable route to simulating fault-tolerant circuits with third-level Clifford hierarchy diagonal gates, whose cost does not grow with the number of logical qubits, making it particularly attractive for large-scale simulations and, via Clifford simulator interfacing, for larger circuits and algorithmic subroutines.

title: Engineering and Probing a One-Dimensional Dipolar Spin Ensemble in Diamond
summary: Dimensionality plays a central role in determining the collective behavior of interacting quantum systems. Engineering strongly interacting ensembles of solid-state spin defects in reduced dimensions remains a significant challenge at the interface between the applied and fundamental sciences. Here, we create and characterize a positionally disordered, quasi-one-dimensional spin chain in diamond, consisting of optically dark substitutional nitrogen defects (P1 centers) and optically addressable probe nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. Our approach exploits the preferential incorporation of nitrogen along step bunches formed during chemical vapor deposition to achieve both lateral and vertical confinement. Combining spatially resolved materials characterization with nanoscale quantum sensing, we establish the one-dimensional character of the optically dark, unpolarized P1 spin ensemble. We then use correlation spectroscopy to probe local spin autocorrelations and investigate infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport. Our results establish a materials-based route for engineering low-dimensional quantum spin systems.

AI.tldr: The authors engineer and characterize a positionally disordered quasi-one-dimensional spin chain in diamond, composed of dark P1 centers and optically addressable NV probe centers, by exploiting preferential nitrogen incorporation along diamond CVD growth step bunches.
AI.motivation: Dimensionality dictates the collective behavior of interacting quantum systems, yet engineering strongly interacting ensembles of solid-state spin defects in reduced dimensions remains a major challenge at the boundary of applied and fundamental science.
AI.method: Nitrogen is preferentially incorporated along step bunches formed during chemical vapor deposition, producing lateral and vertical confinement of P1 (substitutional nitrogen) defects with NV centers as probes; spatially resolved materials characterization is combined with nanoscale quantum sensing to confirm the 1D character of the unpolarized P1 ensemble, and correlation spectroscopy probes local spin autocorrelations and infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport.
AI.result: The optically dark, unpolarized P1 spin ensemble exhibits established one-dimensional character; local spin autocorrelations and infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport are measured via correlation spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a materials-based route for engineering low-dimensional quantum spin systems in diamond.

title: Normalizing Flow-Based Bayesian Parameter Estimation for Noisy Quantum States
summary: To extract complete information about experimental noisy quantum states, as well as correlations among different physical parameters, we develop an efficient machine learning-assisted framework with the normalizing flow based Bayesian parameter estimation (BPE). By embedding a physically interpretable parameter vector, ${s}$, into the quantum state ansatzes, $ρ({s})$, the corresponding parameter distribution $p({s}|D)$ is induced from BPE, based on the available experimental data $D$. The BPE allows us to perform parameter correlation analyses, providing powerful insights about how experimental parameters and related noise sources affect quantum features of the system. As an example, the flexibility of our framework is demonstrated using two different physical ansatzes on the optical cat state experiments, where a noisy single-photon state is added to impure squeezed state. With correlations among the Wigner function negativity, photon-addition fraction, noisy fraction, and pump powers, our framework gives interpretations for complicated experimental mechanisms in generating noisy non-Gaussian states. By leveraging normalizing flow-based neural networks and Bayesian uncertainty estimation, along with physical and experimental constraints incorporated naturally, the valuable information inferred in the posterior learning provides guidelines for experimentalists, as well as theorists, in identifying promising parameters to enhance desirable features.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a machine learning-assisted framework using normalizing flow-based Bayesian parameter estimation (BPE) to extract complete information and correlations among physical parameters from experimental noisy quantum states.
AI.motivation: Extracting complete information about experimental noisy quantum states and correlations among different physical parameters is challenging. Existing methods may not efficiently infer parameter distributions or provide uncertainty estimation and interpretability for complex experimental mechanisms.
AI.method: A physically interpretable parameter vector s is embedded into quantum state ansatzes ρ(s). The parameter distribution p(s|D) is induced via normalizing flow-based Bayesian parameter estimation from experimental data D. This enables parameter correlation analyses. The framework is demonstrated on optical cat state experiments using two different physical ansatzes, where a noisy single-photon state is added to an impure squeezed state.
AI.result: The framework reveals correlations among the Wigner function negativity, photon-addition fraction, noisy fraction, and pump powers, providing interpretations for complicated experimental mechanisms in generating noisy non-Gaussian states. It leverages normalizing flow neural networks and Bayesian uncertainty estimation with physical and experimental constraints naturally incorporated.
AI.conclusion: The posterior learning provides guidelines for experimentalists and theorists in identifying promising parameters to enhance desirable quantum state features, demonstrating the flexibility and power of the ML-assisted BPE framework.

title: Symmetry-driven correlation patterns in one-dimensional periodic fermionic systems: closed-form expressions and exact selection rules for correlation functions, entanglement entropies and mutual information
comment: The following article has been accepted by The Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: We present an analytical study of the spatial structure of correlations in periodic fermionic systems at the single Slater determinant level, focusing on the cyclic case. Exploiting cyclic symmetry, the transformation from localized orbitals to molecular orbitals is simultaneously a discrete Fourier transform, a Vandermonde matrix on the roots of unity, a complex Hadamard matrix, and the character table of the cyclic group $C_m$. Within this framework, the spatial structure of correlations is fully determined by the occupied irreducible representations (Fourier modes), independently of the specific Hamiltonian generating them. In particular, the fermionic two-point correlator is expressed as a truncated Fourier sum over the occupied orbitals, leading to exact analytical expressions for symmetric occupation patterns of Fourier modes ($\ell$ and $-\ell$ pairs), corresponding in quantum chemistry to aromatic fillings, i.e. fillings satisfying Hückel's $4n + 2$ rule. For the half filling case, we derive exact spatial selection rules. In particular, the two-point correlator vanishes identically for all even distances along the ring. This property propagates to reduced density matrices and implies a complete absence of mutual information between the corresponding orbitals. These results reveal that, despite the global delocalization of molecular orbitals, the correlation structure in cyclic systems is highly non-uniform and governed by symmetry-induced interference. Although formulated in terms of cyclic lattice systems, the present results extend straightforwardly to one-dimensional fermionic chains with periodic conditions, reflecting the underlying translational symmetry of the problem. The framework therefore provides a Hamiltonian-independent and universal reference for understanding correlation patterns in one-dimensional periodic fermionic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically studies spatial correlation structure in periodic fermionic (cyclic) systems at the single Slater determinant level, showing correlations are determined solely by occupied Fourier modes and deriving exact selection rules, including vanishing of the two-point correlator at all even distances under half filling.
AI.motivation: Understanding spatial correlations in periodic fermionic systems is typically entangled with the specific Hamiltonian. The authors aim to decouple this dependence and provide a Hamiltonian-independent, universal framework that isolates the role of symmetry in governing correlation patterns.
AI.method: Exploiting cyclic symmetry of the ring, they reinterpret the localized-to-molecular orbital transformation as a discrete Fourier transform, a Vandermonde matrix on roots of unity, a complex Hadamard matrix, and the character table of the cyclic group C_m. The fermionic two-point correlator is expressed as a truncated Fourier sum over occupied orbitals, yielding exact analytical expressions for symmetric occupation patterns (ℓ, −ℓ pairs, i.e. aromatic/Hückel 4n+2 fillings).
AI.result: For symmetric occupation patterns, exact analytical expressions are obtained; at half filling, exact spatial selection rules emerge, with the two-point correlator vanishing identically at all even distances along the ring. This propagates to reduced density matrices and implies complete absence of mutual information between corresponding orbitals. Correlations are highly non-uniform despite global molecular orbital delocalization.
AI.conclusion: The correlation structure in cyclic fermionic systems is governed by symmetry-induced interference and is Hamiltonian-independent. The results extend directly to one-dimensional fermionic chains with periodic boundary conditions, offering a universal reference for correlation patterns in periodic fermionic systems.

title: A Bi-Objective Routing Framework for Hybrid Terrestrial-Satellite Quantum Networks
summary: Hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks combine terrestrial fiber infrastructure with free-space links to enable long-distance entanglement distribution. Entanglement can be routed over different combinations of terrestrial and satellite links, resulting in paths with different entanglement generation rates (EGRs) and fidelities. Existing routing algorithms, however, typically reduce routing to a single-objective problem by optimizing either EGR or fidelity, or by optimizing one while constraining the other, and thus do not explicitly capture the trade-off between the two. In this paper, we present a bi-objective routing framework for hybrid quantum networks that jointly optimizes end-to-end EGR and fidelity. We formulate routing as a Pareto optimization problem and show that it possesses a special mathematical structure: the bottleneck nature of end-to-end EGR and the multiplicative nature of end-to-end fidelity allow the problem to be transformed into a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem. This transformation enables the exact polynomial-time computation of a minimal complete Pareto set using Martins' bicriterion routing algorithm. Our results demonstrate that hybrid networks expose substantially richer Pareto frontiers than terrestrial-only networks and that the proposed framework outperforms representative single-objective routing policies by allowing applications to select paths based on their EGR and fidelity requirements.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a bi-objective routing framework for hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks that jointly optimizes end-to-end entanglement generation rate (EGR) and fidelity, formulated as a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem solved exactly in polynomial time via Martins' algorithm.
AI.motivation: Hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks enable long-distance entanglement distribution by combining fiber and free-space links, yielding paths with differing EGR and fidelity. Existing routing algorithms collapse this into a single-objective problem (optimizing EGR or fidelity, or one constrained by the other), failing to explicitly capture the EGR-fidelity trade-off.
AI.method: Routing is formulated as a Pareto optimization problem. The authors show that the bottleneck nature of end-to-end EGR and the multiplicative nature of end-to-end fidelity allow transformation into a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem, enabling exact polynomial-time computation of a minimal complete Pareto set using Martins' bicriterion routing algorithm.

AI.conclusion: Joint bi-objective optimization of EGR and fidelity is feasible and beneficial for hybrid quantum network routing, providing exact Pareto sets that better support application-specific path selection.

title: Vehicle-Routing Clustering by Sparse Quantum Relaxation
summary: This paper studies the cluster-assignment layer of a cluster-first-route-second decomposition for the capacitated pickup-and-delivery problem with time windows (CPDPTW), instead of a direct route-ordering quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Sample-based subspace diagonalization (SQD) degenerates to best-of-shots for any diagonal optimization Hamiltonian, so a useful transfer to routing requires non-diagonal relaxation. Quantum random access optimization (QRAO) provides this non-diagonality by encoding binary variables through non-commuting quantum random access code (QRAC) observables. CPDPTW-derived conflict graphs expose a routing-specific obstruction because dense objectives and penalty-encoded constraints destroy QRAO compression. We keep the Hamiltonian sparse by encoding only the sparsified objective and enforcing one-hot, capacity, and cluster time-budget feasibility by repair after rounding. We make no quantum-advantage claim. Under strong repair the classical pass alone reaches near-optimal cost at the tested sizes. The result is a regime map linking sparsification, achieved compression, linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) 1-norm, heavy-hex two-qubit depth, sampling drift, and final routing quality on Qiskit Aer, calibrated FakeTorino, and IBM Heron ibm_quebec. Across a 108-row ideal-calibrated-hardware evaluation grid spanning four to twelve pickup-delivery request pairs, the hardware slice has mean gap 0.0016 and mean device-vs-ideal total variation distance (TVD) 0.279; a decoder ablation at sizes six through twelve isolates the non-diagonal signal.

Quantum random access optimization (QRAO) supplies non-diagonality by encoding binary variables via non-commuting QRAC observables. However, routing-derived conflict graphs from CPDPTW present a specific obstruction: dense objectives and penalty-encoded constraints destroy QRAO compression.

Evaluation spans a 108-row ideal-calibrated-hardware grid across four to twelve pickup-delivery request pairs, on Qiskit Aer, calibrated FakeTorino, and IBM Heron ibm_quebec, including a decoder ablation at sizes six through twelve to isolate the non-diagonal signal.

title: Dephasing-Enhanced Response and Phase Transitions in Quantum Boltzmann Samplers
comment: Main 6 pages + SM 31 pages. Main 3 figures + SM 6 figures
summary: Dephasing can drive a quantum Boltzmann sampler into an ordered phase while its programmed probability distribution remains disordered. We trace this transition to an enhanced conditional response: coherence loss changes how each spin responds to its neighbors, and interactions amplify the change. For all-to-all coupling, we establish the stationary transition at finite dephasing. Near criticality, the magnetization distribution depends on the ratio of dephasing strength to the square root of system size, retaining a finite imprint of coherence even as the local coherent correction vanishes. In the strong-dephasing limit on a square lattice, the dynamics generates effective multispin interactions and probability currents, with Ising-like critical statistics. Adjusting the local dissipative update restores the target probability process on arbitrary graphs.

AI.tldr: Dephasing can push a quantum Boltzmann sampler into an ordered phase even though its programmed probability distribution is disordered. The transition arises from enhanced conditional response amplified by interactions, with a finite-dephasing stationary transition under all-to-all coupling and Ising-like criticality in the strong-dephasing lattice limit.
AI.motivation: Quantum Boltzmann samplers are designed to output a programmed (target) probability distribution, typically disordered. The paper addresses how environmental dephasing, an ostensibly unwanted noise source, can nevertheless drive the sampler into an ordered phase without altering the programmed distribution, and seeks to explain the mechanism and critical behavior of this mismatch.
AI.method: The transition is traced to an enhanced conditional response: coherence loss modifies how each spin responds to its neighbors, and interactions amplify this change. The authors analyze all-to-all coupling to establish the stationary transition at finite dephasing, examine near-critical magnetization scaling, and study the strong-dephasing limit on a square lattice where the dynamics generates effective multispin interactions and probability currents. They also modify the local dissipative update to recover the target probability process on arbitrary graphs.
AI.result: For all-to-all coupling a stationary transition occurs at finite dephasing. Near criticality the magnetization distribution depends on the ratio of dephasing strength to the square root of system size, retaining a finite imprint of coherence even as the local coherent correction vanishes. In the strong-dephasing square-lattice limit, effective multispin interactions and probability currents emerge with Ising-like critical statistics. Adjusting the local dissipative update restores the target probability process on arbitrary graphs.
AI.conclusion: Dephasing induces an ordered phase in a quantum Boltzmann sampler whose programmed distribution stays disordered, driven by coherence-modified conditional response. The critical physics is governed by a dephasing-to-size ratio and yields Ising-like statistics in the strong-dephasing lattice limit. Restoring the intended sampling behavior requires tuning the local dissipative update.

title: A Restricted Boltzmann Machine with Quantum-State Visible Units
summary: We construct a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) whose visible input is a quantum state rather than a classical configuration. Each hidden unit carries a trainable quantum template prepared by a parametrized circuit and converts its overlap with the input into a feature. Treating quantum states as high-dimensional continuous visible objects creates nontrivial normalization and scaling problems. We regularize the continuous likelihood and derive two controlled high-dimensional limits, yielding a Hopfield-type network with continuous Hilbert-space patterns and a data-augmented Gram likelihood. The resulting algorithms are compact and use trainable circuit-prepared templates as measurement intermediaries between quantum data and classical optimization. Numerical simulations across several many-body systems demonstrate effective quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum-state RBM where quantum states (not classical configurations) form the visible input, hidden units are parametrized-circuit quantum templates, and overlap-based features yield, via regularized continuous likelihood limits, a Hopfield-type network and a data-augmented Gram likelihood for quantum-phase recognition.
