AI.motivation: Standard RBMs use classical visible configurations; enabling quantum states as continuous high-dimensional visible inputs could let machine learning directly process quantum data, but treating quantum states this way creates nontrivial normalization and scaling problems that must be resolved.
AI.method: Construct a restricted Boltzmann machine with a quantum state as the visible input. Each hidden unit carries a trainable quantum template prepared by a parametrized circuit, and its overlap with the input is converted into a feature. The continuous likelihood is regularized, and two controlled high-dimensional limits are derived: one giving a Hopfield-type network with continuous Hilbert-space patterns, and one giving a data-augmented Gram likelihood. The resulting algorithms use circuit-prepared templates as measurement intermediaries between quantum data and classical optimization.
AI.result: Numerical simulations across several many-body systems demonstrate effective quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-visible RBM admits well-defined high-dimensional limits, yielding compact algorithms that bridge quantum data and classical optimization through trainable circuit-prepared templates, and empirically support quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction in many-body systems.

title: Experimental certification of the nonlocal advantages of quantum imaginarity
comment: [10] pages, [6] figures. Accepted by Physical Review A. DOI: 10.1103/7jcn-yq29
summary: Quantum imaginarity is a distinct resource in quantum information theory, yet its nonlocal properties have not been fully explored. Here, we report an experimental study of the nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity (NAQI), in which local measurements on one subsystem can steer the average imaginarity of the conditional states of the other subsystem beyond the corresponding classical bound. The $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality is adopted as an experimentally accessible witness. A hybrid optimization algorithm that combines a genetic algorithm with sequential quadratic programming is developed to avoid local optima and accelerate the search for optimal measurement settings. Using polarization-encoded photonic qubits, we prepare two classes of two-qubit Bell-diagonal states and experimentally characterize the imaginarity of the conditional states following local measurements. Clear violations of the $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality are observed, providing an experimental certification of NAQI. We further investigate the relationship among NAQI, the nonlocal advantage of quantum coherence (NAQC), and Bell nonlocality based on their respective inequality criteria. For the two-qubit Werner states considered in this work, the regions of states that violate the respective criteria satisfy $\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQC}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQI}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm BN}$. Our work provides an experimental realization of NAQI and a comparison of different forms of quantum nonclassicality in a photonic platform.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates the nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity (NAQI) using polarization-encoded photonic qubits, verified via violation of an l1-norm of imaginarity inequality.
AI.motivation: Quantum imaginarity is a distinct quantum resource, but its nonlocal properties remained largely unexplored. The authors aim to experimentally realize and certify the nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity and compare it with other forms of quantum nonclassicality.
AI.method: The authors use the l1-norm of imaginarity inequality as an experimentally accessible witness. They develop a hybrid optimization algorithm combining a genetic algorithm with sequential quadratic programming to avoid local optima and accelerate the search for optimal measurement settings. Using polarization-encoded photonic qubits, they prepare two classes of two-qubit Bell-diagonal states and characterize the imaginarity of the conditional states after local measurements.
AI.result: Clear violations of the l1-norm of imaginarity inequality are observed, providing experimental certification of NAQI. For the two-qubit Werner states, the sets of states violating the respective criteria satisfy the hierarchy D_NAQC ⊂ D_NAQI ⊂ D_BN.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an experimental realization of NAQI and a comparison of different forms of quantum nonclassicality (NAQI, NAQC, and Bell nonlocality) in a photonic platform, revealing a nested hierarchy of the corresponding inequality-violating regions.

title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
summary: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is fundamentally a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, and proposes a scalable QPU design blueprint modeled on classical computing and networking principles.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers are novel and unusual, yet at system scale they should be engineered using principles governing classical heterogeneous accelerators. The paper frames scalable quantum architecture as a cost-performance optimization problem.
AI.method: The authors propose an architecture blueprint organized around clean logical abstractions that hide physical qubit modality details below the ISA boundary, aggressively specialize recurring functions to minimize cost for utility-scale quantum computations, and implement low-level control, readout, and QEC via specialized local hardware resembling high-performance network stacks.
AI.result: The design principles and resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking, yielding a blueprint for scalable QPU design.
AI.conclusion: Utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem, and its design can and should leverage established classical computing and networking principles.

title: Improving Sample Efficiency in Peptide-HLA Binding Prediction with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks
summary: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is a critical step in neoantigen identification for personalized cancer immunotherapy and holds significant clinical value. However, the training data available for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, which severely constrains the performance of conventional methods on this task. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases beneficial for learning from small datasets, yet their application to biological sequence prediction remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) specifically designed for peptide-HLA binding prediction. HQNN integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. On two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN outperforms a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablation studies confirm the respective contributions of the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. In noise-aware simulations, performance degrades only mildly, and such degradation is reasonable and acceptable under realistic quantum hardware noise levels. These results suggest that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.

AI.tldr: HQNN, a hybrid quantum-classical neural network combining multi-source biological feature encoding, parallel quantum feature extractors, and a quantum-enhanced classifier, improves peptide-HLA binding prediction over a parameter-matched classical CNN, with the largest gains in low-data regimes and only mild degradation under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is critical for neoantigen identification in personalized cancer immunotherapy, but training data for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, severely constraining conventional methods. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases favorable for small-data learning, yet their use in biological sequence prediction is underexplored.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) integrating multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. Evaluated on two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), with parameter-matched classical CNN baselines, ablation studies, and noise-aware simulations.
AI.result: HQNN outperforms the parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes on both alleles, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablations confirm contributions of both the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. Under noise-aware simulation, performance degrades only mildly and remains reasonable at realistic hardware noise levels.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical architectures can deliver practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes, supporting their value for peptide-HLA binding prediction and personalized cancer immunotherapy.

title: Linear combination of Schrödingerization for quantum linear systems with optimal matrix-query complexity
summary: Quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) aim to solve linear systems $A\bb{x}=\bb{b}$ exponentially faster than classical methods under certain conditions. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for solving linear algebraic equations from an ODE-based perspective. Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach \cite{Childs2017QLSA}, we express the solution $\bb{x}$ as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain. We refer to this representation as LC-Schrödingerization. Based on this result, we construct an LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval. This permits a truncation time independent of the target accuracy and avoids the loss in success probability from selecting a single grid point. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients provide the corresponding projection error bounds. Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity $\mathcal{O}(κ_A\log\frac1\varepsilon)$ without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.

AI.tldr: The paper develops quantum algorithms for linear systems $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ from an ODE perspective, introducing an "LC-Schrödingerization" that expresses the solution as a linear combination of linear convection/Schrödinger-type equations, and constructs an LCHS-based algorithm achieving optimal matrix-query complexity $\mathcal{O}(\kappa_A \log 1/\varepsilon)$ without variable-time amplitude amplification.
AI.motivation: QLSAs promise exponential speedup over classical linear solvers under certain conditions, but existing approaches (e.g., HHL and Fourier-based LCHS methods) face limitations such as success-probability loss from selecting a single grid point and reliance on variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The authors seek an ODE-based reformulation that avoids these issues while retaining optimal query complexity.
AI.method: Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach, the solution $\mathbf{x}$ is expressed as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain (LC-Schrödingerization). An LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances is constructed: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval, enabling a truncation time independent of target accuracy and avoiding single-grid-point success-probability loss. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients give projection error bounds.
AI.result: Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity $\mathcal{O}(\kappa_A \log 1/\varepsilon)$ without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.
AI.conclusion: The ODE-based LC-Schrödingerization yields a QLSA with optimal matrix-query complexity, matching the best known bounds while avoiding VTAA and the success-probability loss inherent in single-grid-point selection, with the same guarantee applying to right-hand-side oracle queries.

title: Exact Local Optimality Does Not Compose: The Complexity of Chronological Realization
summary:
The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is the smallest normalized stochastic state dimension $C_{\rm seq}$ needed to reproduce a collection of future-response menus using one shared family of controlled transition dynamics. We focus on the rank-tight regime in which both the local realization dimension and the independent-query static carrier width equal $K$, thereby isolating the additional dimensional and computational constraints imposed by chronological consistency. This framework also serves as the classical baseline for state-dimension bounds in sequential quantum processes, where stochastic dynamics generalize to completely positive maps.
  We establish three results in this regime. First, an explicit payload--delay family exhibits an unbounded multiplicative state blow-up: $C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=k$ while $C_{\rm seq}=k(L+1)$, isolating the intrinsic state cost of shared temporal pullbacks. Second, for explicitly listed rational finite menus over a fixed five-letter alphabet with a single Boolean terminal effect, exact shared realizability is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete, and the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial defect promise problem is $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$-complete, with local and static optima fixed at $K$. Third, a total five-letter chronology compiler translates bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances into a polynomially specified regular geometric family over the same fixed alphabet, preserving exact local and static width $K$. The compiled family yields strong $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$-hardness for shared realization on strongly bounded-rational inputs, together with an $\exists\mathbb{R}$ upper bound certified by an exact polynomial-size finite core. Together, these results show that exact local and static optimality need not compose under chronological sharing, even in the rank-tight regime.

AI.tldr: The paper studies chronological shared realization complexity (CRC), the minimal normalized stochastic state dimension needed to reproduce future-response menus via shared controlled transition dynamics. In the rank-tight regime (local and static width both equal K), it shows that local and static optimality do not compose under chronological sharing, proving an unbounded state blow-up, ∃ℝ-completeness of exact shared realizability, and PromiseNP-completeness/hardness results.
AI.motivation: Local and static realization dimensions are individually well understood, but the extra cost imposed by requiring a single shared family of controlled dynamics across a chronological sequence of queries is not. This paper isolates that cost in the rank-tight regime where local and static dimensions both equal K, thereby separating chronological consistency constraints from ordinary static dimension bounds. The framework also serves as the classical baseline for state-dimension bounds in sequential quantum processes, where stochastic dynamics generalize to completely positive maps.
AI.method: The analysis focuses on the rank-tight regime with fixed five-letter alphabet, a single Boolean terminal effect, and rational finite menus. Three constructions are used: (1) an explicit payload-delay family of menus; (2) reduction from Intermediate Simplex / strongly bounded-rational instances; (3) a total five-letter chronology compiler translating bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances into a polynomially specified regular geometric family over the same alphabet while preserving exact local and static width K. Complexity classifications are established via ∃ℝ and PromiseNP reductions, with an exact polynomial-size finite core certifying the ∃ℝ upper bound.
AI.result: Three main results: (1) An explicit payload-delay family exhibits unbounded multiplicative state blow-up, with C_loc = C_stat = k while C_seq = k(L+1), isolating the intrinsic state cost of shared temporal pullbacks. (2) For explicitly listed rational finite menus over a fixed five-letter alphabet with a single Boolean terminal effect, exact shared realizability is ∃ℝ-complete, and the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial defect promise problem is PromiseNP-complete, with local and static optima fixed at K. (3) The total five-letter chronology compiler yields strong PromiseNP-hardness for shared realization on strongly bounded-rational inputs, together with an ∃ℝ upper bound certified by an exact polynomial-size finite core.
AI.conclusion: Exact local and static optimality need not compose under chronological sharing, even in the rank-tight regime: shared realizability can require strictly larger state dimension than either local or static realization, and deciding it is computationally hard (∃ℝ-complete / PromiseNP-complete). The results delineate the intrinsic dimensional and computational cost of chronological consistency and provide a classical baseline for state-dimension bounds in sequential quantum processes.

title: Scalable entanglement distribution using encoded hybrid repeater chains
comment: 28 pages main text (plus 14 pages Appendix), 12 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: Long-distance entanglement distribution requires error correction protocols to compensate for qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise introduced during entanglement swapping. We argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates. Taking the resource-intensive nature of hybrid nodes into account, we propose and analyze repeater chains in which only a subset of nodes need to be hybrid, while the remaining nodes are simpler first-generation repeaters with no error-correction capability. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the $[[7,1,3]]$ Steane code, and the $[[9,1,3]]$ Shor code, we demonstrate that these hybrid architectures outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate. In our study we develop a full circuit-level noise model of our architectures and examine the impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms on our hybrid architecture. We also develop a modified version of the swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing, more suited to our architecture where some nodes perform error-correction while others do not. This modified policy significantly reduces the information storage time in memory qubits relative to the previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum repeater chains that combine fast type-1 memories with high-coherence type-2 memories at only a subset of nodes outperform single-platform architectures in end-to-end entanglement distribution rate, as shown via Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant repetition, Steane, and Shor code protocols.
AI.motivation: Long-distance entanglement distribution suffers from qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise from entanglement swapping, requiring error correction. Single-platform repeater chains are limited because no one memory technology combines fast entanglement generation with long coherence times and low gate errors. The paper argues for exploiting complementary strengths of multiple physical platforms, while addressing the high resource cost of fully hybrid nodes.
AI.method: The authors propose hybrid repeater architectures combining type-1 memories (fast entanglement generation, multiplexing-suitable) and type-2 memories (long coherence, low two-qubit gate error). Only a subset of nodes are hybrid, with remaining nodes being simpler first-generation repeaters lacking error correction. They build a circuit-level noise model and run detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the [[7,1,3]] Steane code, and the [[9,1,3]] Shor code. They also examine the effect of an imperfect interface between the two platforms and develop a modified swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing suited to partially error-corrected chains.
AI.result: Hybrid architectures achieve higher end-to-end entanglement distribution rates than pure single-platform architectures. The imperfect interface between platforms is analyzed for its impact. The modified swap-as-soon-as-possible policy substantially reduces information storage time in memory qubits compared to previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary quantum memory platforms in hybrid repeater chains, even when only a subset of nodes is hybrid, improves entanglement distribution performance. The proposed modified swapping policy lowers memory storage demands, making such partially hybrid, error-corrected repeater architectures practical and advantageous over single-platform designs.

title: Transduction-Enabled Superconducting Quantum Repeater: Toward Deterministic Entanglement Distribution with High-Fidelity Gates
summary: Long-distance entanglement distribution is hindered by photon loss in optical fibers and the nocloning theorem. Optical quantum repeater (QR) protocols rely on Bell state measurements (BSMs), they are intrinsically limited to probabilistic photon operations and fail 50% of the time. We propose a hybrid approach to building quantum repeaters that combines the high transmission speed of photonic qubits in optical fiber with the high-fidelity quantum processing capabilities enabled by superconducting circuits. The transduction-enabled superconducting QR (TESQR) architecture eliminates the need for probabilistic BSMs and allows deterministic processing operations. The TESQR framework always yields a final state at the remote nodes rather than aborting on photon loss, manifesting deterministic entanglement distribution within certain parameter regimes. We evaluate the performance by assessing output-state fidelities and success probabilities of entanglement distribution using realistic noise models. Additionally, we integrate an entanglement purification scheme and evaluate the performance through numerical simulations in QuTiP environment. Our results show that, for entanglement swapping, the proposed scheme improves the entanglement distribution rate by an average of 63% and by up to 159% compared with photonic-only architectures. Moreover, after purification, the end-to-end fidelities exceed 0.8 over distances up to 20 km.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transduction-enabled superconducting quantum repeater (TESQR) architecture that replaces probabilistic Bell state measurements with deterministic processing, achieving up to 159% higher entanglement distribution rates than photonic-only schemes and end-to-end fidelities above 0.8 up to 20 km after purification.
AI.motivation: Long-distance entanglement distribution is limited by photon loss in optical fibers and the no-cloning theorem. Existing optical quantum repeater protocols rely on Bell state measurements, which are intrinsically probabilistic, fail 50% of the time, and abort on photon loss, motivating a hybrid design that avoids these probabilistic operations.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum repeater combining high-speed photonic qubits in fiber with high-fidelity superconducting processing via transduction. The TESQR architecture eliminates probabilistic BSMs, enables deterministic processing, and always produces a final state at remote nodes instead of aborting on loss. Performance is evaluated with realistic noise models, and an entanglement purification scheme is integrated, with numerical simulations in QuTiP.
AI.result: For entanglement swapping, the scheme improves the entanglement distribution rate by an average of 63% and by up to 159% compared with photonic-only architectures. After purification, end-to-end fidelities exceed 0.8 over distances up to 20 km.
AI.conclusion: The TESQR approach enables deterministic entanglement distribution within certain parameter regimes and outperforms photonic-only repeaters in both rate and fidelity, offering a viable path toward long-distance quantum networking.

title: 90%-Efficient Optical Storage in a Rare-Earth Crystal with a Low-Loss Impedance-Matched Cavity
summary: High-efficiency optical storage in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals is challenging because of their typically weak optical absorption,which makes cavity-enhanced memories highly sensitive to parasitic intracavity loss. Here we demonstrate a 90.1(5)% storage efficiency for coherent optical pulses in an impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory based on Eu3+:Y2SiO5. The Brewster-angle configuration of the crystal and fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity reduce the round-trip intracavity loss to 0.37%. Quantitative modeling shows that further improvement is limited primarily by AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response rather than by residual cavity loss,identifying the principal requirements for further approaching unity efficiency.

AI.tldr: A 90.1(5)% storage efficiency for coherent optical pulses is demonstrated in an impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory using Eu3+:Y2SiO5, with round-trip intracavity loss reduced to 0.37% via a Brewster-angle, fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity; modeling shows AFC preparation, not residual loss, now limits performance.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals suffer from weak optical absorption, making cavity-enhanced memories highly sensitive to parasitic intracavity loss; high storage efficiency is therefore difficult to achieve.
AI.method: An impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb (AFC) memory based on Eu3+:Y2SiO5, employing a Brewster-angle crystal configuration and a fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity to minimize round-trip intracavity loss, combined with quantitative modeling.
AI.result: Storage efficiency of 90.1(5)% for coherent optical pulses; round-trip intracavity loss reduced to 0.37%. Modeling indicates further improvement is limited primarily by AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response rather than residual cavity loss.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies the principal requirements for approaching unity storage efficiency, establishing AFC preparation quality as the dominant remaining limitation in cavity-enhanced rare-earth quantum memories.

title: Local unitary equivalence of orthogonal arrays and related linear codes
summary: Orthogonal arrays (OAs) are combinatorial configurations with applications in experimental design, error-correcting codes, and quantum information. Local unitary (LU) equivalence provides a natural framework for classifying multipartite entangled states. Using the correspondence between OAs and quantum states, Goyeneche and Życzkowski [Phys. Rev. A, 2014, 90: 022316] posed the problem of determining when OAs are $LU$ equivalent. In this paper, we construct OAs from generator matrices and establish conditions for Fourier-based $LU$ equivalence of OAs and irredundant orthogonal arrays (IrOAs). For prime alphabets, we identify the Fourier partners of the linear OAs considered here with the arrays of their corresponding dual codes. This gives an explicit connection between $LU$ equivalence and coding theory. We also identify families of $LU$ equivalent OAs arising from specific classes of linear codes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies when orthogonal arrays are locally unitarily equivalent by constructing OAs from generator matrices and linking Fourier-based LU equivalence to dual codes for prime alphabets.
AI.motivation: Goyeneche and Życzkowski posed the problem of determining when orthogonal arrays are LU equivalent. This paper aims to address this classification problem using the OA-quantum state correspondence.
AI.method: The authors construct OAs from generator matrices and establish conditions for Fourier-based LU equivalence of OAs and irredundant orthogonal arrays (IrOAs). For prime alphabets, they identify Fourier partners of linear OAs with arrays of corresponding dual codes.
AI.result: For prime alphabets, Fourier partners of the considered linear OAs are identified with the arrays of their dual codes, giving an explicit connection between LU equivalence and coding theory. Families of LU equivalent OAs arising from specific classes of linear codes are also identified.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes conditions for Fourier-based LU equivalence of OAs and IrOAs, connects LU equivalence to coding theory via dual codes for prime alphabets, and identifies families of LU equivalent OAs from linear codes.

title: Long-horizon autoformalization of a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE
comment: 72 pages. Main text 13 pages with 4 figures and 1 table, followed by supplementary appendices (57 pages, 9 figures, 17 tables) and references. Lean 4 library: https://github.com/LionSR/MIPStarRE
summary: Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving and review loops. Agents strengthen verification and review throughout formalization. We completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE. Developing the proof took 63 days; greater parallelism could further reduce this time. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. The formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate errors while preserving the published final error bound under corrected assumptions. This work provides a verified foundation for quantum complexity and demonstrates a route to affordable verification of major research proofs by small teams.

AI.tldr: FormalFlow coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to formalize long-horizon mathematical proofs, addressing statement drift and proof composition. Applied to Lean 4, it produced a machine-checked proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test (a core theorem beneath MIP* = RE) in 63 days, yielding 126,367 lines of agent-generated Lean code.
AI.motivation: Landmark mathematical formalizations have historically required specialist teams years to complete, making large-scale verification costly and inaccessible to small teams. Long-horizon formalization also suffers from statement drift (divergence between the intended statement and what is actually proven) and difficulty in composing proofs, while the quantum complexity foundation underlying results such as MIP* = RE lacks a verified formal basis.
AI.method: FormalFlow coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision, drawing on software engineering principles. A shared blueprint guides nested planning, proving, and review loops, and agents strengthen verification and review throughout the formalization process to mitigate statement drift and support proof composition. The system was applied to produce a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test.
AI.result: The formalization of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test in Lean 4 took 63 days, with greater parallelism offering further time reduction. The final library comprises 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. The process corrected side conditions and intermediate errors while preserving the published final error bound under corrected assumptions.
AI.conclusion: FormalFlow provides a verified foundation for quantum complexity and demonstrates a route to affordable verification of major research proofs by small teams, showing that coordinated AI proving agents under human supervision can complete long-horizon formalizations that previously demanded years of specialist effort.

title: Automated search for highly contextual Kochen-Specker proofs
summary: Observable-based Kochen-Specker proofs are configurations of multi-qubit Pauli observables grouped into contexts whose products are plus or minus the indentity. Their robustness as state-independent contextuality tests can be measured by the tolerated error per context $\varepsilon = 2d/|H|$, where $d$ is the contextuality degree and $|H|$ the number of contexts. Since the degree depends only on an underlying abstract structure called the hypergram i.e. the pair formed by the context hypergraph and the anticommutation graph, the search for highly contextual proofs can be carried out on them instead, with no reference to qubits or to any particular Pauli labeling. We further exploit this by enumerating anticommutation graphs first, and then by associating to each graph $G$ the single hypergram carrying its entire hypergraph support $HS(G)$, so that exactly one candidate is examined per graph. Applied to the House of Graphs database and to censuses of vertex-transitive graphs on at most 24 vertices, this pipeline recovers the Peres-Mermin square, the doily and the Mermin pentagram, and yields configurations reaching $\varepsilon = 0.707$, against $0.424$ for the previous published record. The best configurations are predominantly those stemming from line graphs and unions of graphs; we explain the former by showing that every perfect matching of a graph is a context of its line graph, which exhibits the Peres-Mermin square and the doily as the first members of two infinite families. We close with finite geometric descriptions of the most striking configurations inside symplectic polar spaces, in terms of ovoids, hyperbolic quadrics and Fano planes.

AI.tldr: Observable-based Kochen-Specker proofs are recast as hypergrams (context hypergraph plus anticommutation graph), enabling a qubit-free enumeration that finds configurations with a tolerated context error of 0.707, surpassing the previous record of 0.424.
AI.motivation: Robustness of state-independent contextuality tests is quantified by the tolerated error per context ε = 2d/|H|, which depends only on the abstract hypergram, motivating a search for highly contextual proofs without reference to qubits or specific Pauli labelings.
AI.method: Enumerate anticommutation graphs first, then associate to each graph G the single hypergram carrying its entire hypergraph support HS(G), so that exactly one candidate is examined per graph. Applied to the House of Graphs database and censuses of vertex-transitive graphs on at most 24 vertices; line graphs and graph unions are analyzed, with finite geometric descriptions inside symplectic polar spaces.
AI.result: The pipeline recovers the Peres-Mermin square, the doily, and the Mermin pentagram, and yields configurations reaching ε = 0.707 versus 0.424 for the previous published record. Best configurations predominantly stem from line graphs and unions of graphs; every perfect matching of a graph is shown to be a context of its line graph, exhibiting the Peres-Mermin square and the doily as first members of two infinite families.
AI.conclusion: A hypergram-based, qubit-free enumeration efficiently discovers highly robust state-independent contextuality proofs, identifies line graphs and unions as the dominant source of optimal configurations, and characterizes the most striking configurations geometrically via ovoids, hyperbolic quadrics, and Fano planes.

title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
summary: Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark for evaluating NISQ and fault-tolerant quantum computers on graph nodefinding via discrete-time quantum walks and amplitude amplification, scoring by the largest solvable problem size.
AI.motivation: Recent progress in quantum hardware toward fault-tolerance has raised interest in assessing near-term platforms on application-relevant algorithms, creating a need for a scalable, application-oriented benchmark.
AI.method: QWS is built on essential quantum routines—discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification—to solve the graph nodefinding (marked-vertex search) problem. Performance is quantified by the largest problem size for which a designated target node is found with success probability above a defined threshold. The paper also gives parameter-selection scenarios derived from noiseless simulations.
AI.result: The benchmark is demonstrated through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors, alongside example parameter-selection scenarios based on noiseless simulations.
AI.conclusion: QWS offers a scalable, application-oriented means to benchmark NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers on graph nodefinding tasks.

title: Quantum Graph Convolutional Networks: Implementation and Trainability Analysis
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph-structured data, but training and inference on large graphs are often bottlenecked by memory constraints and sparse linear-algebra workloads. Quantum computing offers an alternative set of primitives that may improve scalability for graph learning. Building on the quantum graph neural network (QGNN) framework of Liao \textit{et al.}, this work implements two representative architectures --- the Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC) models --- and evaluates them on open benchmark graph datasets and semi-supervised learning tasks using quantum simulation. We compare predictive performance and optimization behavior against classical baselines, showing that the quantum models achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters. Finally, we present a cost gradient analysis that identifies the tasks for which the models showcased are trainable. This is followed by a classical simulability study to find regimes in which the proposed circuits remain robust during training.

AI.tldr: This work implements quantum versions of SGC and LGC graph convolution models within the QGNN framework, benchmarking them against classical baselines on semi-supervised graph tasks, and analyzes cost gradients and classical simulability to characterize trainability and robustness.
AI.motivation: Classical GNN training and inference on large graphs are bottlenecked by memory constraints and sparse linear-algebra workloads. Quantum computing offers alternative primitives that may improve scalability for graph learning, motivating a quantum approach to graph convolution.
AI.method: Building on the quantum graph neural network (QGNN) framework of Liao et al., the authors implement two representative architectures—Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC)—and evaluate them via quantum simulation on open benchmark graph datasets and semi-supervised learning tasks, comparing predictive performance and optimization behavior against classical baselines. They additionally perform a cost gradient analysis and a classical simulability study.
AI.result: The quantum models achieve competitive predictive performance relative to classical baselines while using fewer parameters. The cost gradient analysis identifies the tasks for which the showcased models are trainable, and the classical simulability study delineates regimes in which the proposed circuits remain robust during training.
AI.conclusion: Quantum SGC and LGC architectures are viable, parameter-efficient alternatives for graph learning, with trainability and robustness regimes characterized by cost gradient and classical simulability analyses.

title: Semiclassical scaling of eigenstate thermalization in single-particle chaotic systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 3 pages, 1 figure
summary: We study the off-diagonal matrix elements of real-space observables in time-reversal-invariant single-particle chaotic systems. By analyzing the semiclassical expression for the off-diagonal variance derived from Berry's conjecture, we show that the banded structure of the observable matrix emerges naturally. For local observables, we identify a characteristic bandwidth associated with a late-time timescale inversely proportional to the particle velocity. We further show that, for systems with steep-wall confinement, the predicted magnitude follows the entropy scaling of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), multiplied by an additional kinetic-energy-dependent factor that is independent of spatial dimension and is not captured by conventional many-body ETH. We illustrate these results through a case study of quantum billiards and verify the semiclassical scaling numerically in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard. Our results elucidate the dynamical implications of Berry's conjecture and provide a comparison between single-particle eigenstate thermalization and many-body ETH.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze off-diagonal matrix elements of real-space observables in time-reversal-invariant single-particle chaotic systems, showing that Berry's conjecture semiclassically yields a natural banded structure, a velocity-determined bandwidth, and an ETH-like scaling with an extra kinetic-energy factor, verified numerically in a quantum billiard.
AI.motivation: Off-diagonal matrix elements govern the dynamics of observables and underpin the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), yet their structure in single-particle chaotic systems—especially the emergence of banding and the precise scaling of the variance—remains insufficiently understood, particularly how single-particle eigenstate thermalization relates to conventional many-body ETH.
AI.method: Starting from Berry's conjecture, the authors derive the semiclassical expression for the off-diagonal variance of real-space observables in time-reversal-invariant single-particle chaotic systems. They analyze its structure to extract banding and bandwidth, and for steep-wall confined systems compare the predicted magnitude against ETH entropy scaling. They illustrate the results with quantum billiards and test the semiclassical scaling numerically in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard.
AI.result: The banded structure of the observable matrix emerges naturally from Berry's conjecture. Local observables exhibit a characteristic bandwidth tied to a late-time timescale inversely proportional to the particle velocity. For steep-wall confinement, the predicted magnitude follows ETH entropy scaling multiplied by an additional kinetic-energy-dependent factor that is independent of spatial dimension and absent from conventional many-body ETH. Numerical simulations in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard confirm the semiclassical scaling.
AI.conclusion: The work clarifies the dynamical implications of Berry's conjecture by explaining how banded observable matrices and velocity-set bandwidths arise, and provides a quantitative comparison between single-particle eigenstate thermalization and many-body ETH, highlighting an extra dimension-independent kinetic-energy factor in the single-particle case.

title: Private communication from Pauli channels with no privacy
summary: A channel capacity quantifies the communication capability of a noisy physical process. In contrast to communication channels in the classical world, quantum theory makes this capability contextual. We show that two Pauli two-qubit channels, each with zero private classical capacity, can be used to transmit private information when used together. One is a two-qubit Pauli channel whose environment can reconstruct the receiver output up to matrix transposition; the other is an antidegradable channel. We obtain a similar result when the second channel is the 50% qubit erasure channel. A simple binary code built from rank-three mixtures of Bell states activates private communication. The main ingredient in our construction is a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable.

AI.tldr: Two Pauli two-qubit channels, each individually possessing zero private classical capacity, can jointly transmit private information when combined, exhibiting superactivation of private communication.
AI.motivation: Channel capacity quantifies the communication capability of a noisy physical process. Unlike classical channels, quantum channels make this capability contextual, motivating the investigation of whether channels with zero private classical capacity individually can transmit private information when combined.
AI.method: The authors combine two Pauli two-qubit channels: one whose environment can reconstruct the receiver output up to matrix transposition, and either an antidegradable channel or the 50% qubit erasure channel. They construct a simple binary code from rank-three mixtures of Bell states, with the key ingredient being a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable.
AI.result: Two Pauli two-qubit channels, each with zero private classical capacity, can jointly transmit private information. The same effect is obtained when the second channel is the 50% qubit erasure channel. A simple binary code built from rank-three Bell-state mixtures activates private communication.
AI.conclusion: Private communication can be activated by combining channels that individually have zero private classical capacity, revealing a superactivation phenomenon enabled by a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable.

title: Electrostatic Stabilization of Near-Surface Quantum Sensors via Dielectric Interface Engineering
summary: Control of charge-state stability in near-surface quantum defects is critical for nanoscale sensing, yet remains particularly challenging under ultra-high vacuum (UHV), where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge-state. Here, we present a robust and reproducible approach for stabilizing shallowly implanted (< 10 nm deep) nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in near-UHV conditions (P = $3 \times 10^{-9}$ mbar) based on dielectric interface engineering. Through measurements on individually addressable NV centers, we demonstrate that a TiO2 coating on the diamond suppresses surface-induced electrostatic fields, yielding a 79% increase n NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV-spin resonance contrast at room temperature. Coherent control measurements further reveal suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics. These results establish dielectric screening as a powerful and reproducible strategy to engineer charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: A TiO2 dielectric coating on diamond stabilizes near-surface NV centers under UHV conditions, increasing NV- population by 79% and spin resonance contrast by 45%.
AI.motivation: Charge-state stability of near-surface quantum defects is essential for nanoscale sensing but is hard to maintain under UHV, where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge state.
AI.method: Dielectric interface engineering using a TiO2 coating on diamond, tested on individually addressable shallowly implanted (<10 nm deep) NV centers under near-UHV conditions (P = 3 × 10^-9 mbar), with measurements of NV- population, spin resonance contrast, and coherent control.
AI.result: The TiO2 coating suppresses surface-induced electrostatic fields, producing a 79% increase in NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV-spin resonance contrast at room temperature, while coherent control measurements reveal suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Dielectric screening is established as a powerful, reproducible strategy for engineering the charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.

title: Exceptional points and Jordan-chain signatures in quantum first-passage statistics
summary: Exceptional-point signatures in first-passage observables are governed by two independent survival mechanisms: nonlinear spectral defectivity must pass from the one-record or transfer description to the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and the resulting ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with the chosen preparation and terminal observation. For finite reset-form monitored quantum systems with upward-skip-free counting, we prove the exact threshold factorization $H_N(s)=R_s^N$, identify the physical Perron branch, and derive the transfer factorization $Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI)$. Invertibility of the cofactor gives local equality of Smith data, whereas a singular cofactor can contribute transfer multiplicity absent from the ladder. An order-two Keldysh formula yields an independent observation gate. We then prove a fixed-reset no-go theorem: even a defective full tilted generator cannot generate a cumulative-count Jordan polynomial when the post-count ladder is scalar. Finally, we construct a three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness, minimal within irreducible nonnegative ladders, with a genuine subleading $Nλ^N$ threshold term and a coherence-tuned model in which a binary terminal effect retains the exact polynomial signature at a transversal transform-domain exceptional point. The analysis is formulated at the level of exact transform-domain structure; time-domain asymptotics and perturbative robustness remain separate questions.

AI.tldr: Exceptional-point (EP) signatures in first-passage observables require two independent survival mechanisms: transfer-level spectral defectivity must be imprinted onto the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and the resulting ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with preparation and terminal observation. The paper proves exact threshold and transfer factorizations, derives a Keldysh-based observation gate, establishes a fixed-reset no-go theorem, and constructs a minimal three-reset witness with a genuine subleading Jordan term.
AI.motivation: EP signatures in first-passage (counting) observables are often expected naively from spectral defectivity, but defectivity at the transfer or one-record level need not appear in the physical first-passage statistics. The paper aims to isolate the precise conditions under which EP signatures do or do not survive into observable first-passage quantities, and to clarify how reset/monitoring structure controls this passage.
AI.method: Analysis is carried out at the exact transform-domain level. The authors study finite reset-form monitored quantum systems with upward-skip-free counting, prove an exact threshold factorization H_N(s)=R_s^N, identify the physical Perron branch, and derive a transfer factorization Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI). They compare Smith data via cofactor invertibility, use an order-two Keldysh formula as an independent observation gate, prove a fixed-reset no-go theorem, and construct a three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness plus a coherence-tuned model with a transversal transform-domain EP.
AI.result: Exact threshold factorization H_N(s)=R_s^N and transfer factorization Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI) are proven. Invertibility of the cofactor yields local equality of Smith data, while a singular cofactor can contribute transfer multiplicity absent from the ladder. The order-two Keldysh formula provides a separate observation gate. A fixed-reset no-go theorem shows that even a defective full tilted generator cannot generate a cumulative-count Jordan polynomial when the post-count ladder is scalar. A minimal three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness is built within irreducible nonnegative ladders, exhibiting a genuine subleading Nλ^N threshold term, and a coherence-tuned binary terminal model retains the exact polynomial signature at a transversal transform-domain EP.
AI.conclusion: EP signatures in first-passage observables are governed by two independent survival mechanisms: (i) nonlinear spectral defectivity must pass from the one-record/transfer description to the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and (ii) the resulting ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with both the chosen preparation and terminal observation. The results are formulated at the exact transform-domain level; time-domain asymptotics and perturbative robustness remain open separate questions.

title: Rydberg quantum antennas for chip-interfaced single-photon source array
summary: We propose a Rydberg quantum antenna, consisting of a one-dimensional chain of neutral atoms trapped in a standing-wave optical tweezer, as a chip-interfaced single-photon source. Rydberg blockade induces a single collective excitation in the atomic chain, while its ordered geometry shapes the photon emission into a directional beam, thereby realizing a quantum antenna that emits strictly one photon at a time. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate single-photon collection efficiencies into a waveguide exceeding 70\% through a high-NA lens with a negligible multiple excitation probability. These performance are robust against probabilistic atom loading in the standing-wave dipole traps, requiring only ten atoms, indicating experimental feasibility. The Rydberg quantum antenna thus offers a unique route toward scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, and identical single-photon sources interfaced with a photonic chip, addressing key challenges in photonic quantum information technology.

AI.tldr: A Rydberg quantum antenna—a 1D chain of neutral atoms in a standing-wave optical tweezer—acts as a chip-interfaced single-photon source, achieving >70% single-photon collection efficiency via Rydberg blockade-induced single collective excitation and directional emission.
AI.motivation: Photonic quantum information technology requires scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, identical single-photon sources interfaced with photonic chips, which remains a key challenge.
AI.method: Propose a Rydberg quantum antenna: a 1D chain of neutral atoms trapped in a standing-wave optical tweezer. Rydberg blockade creates a single collective excitation in the chain, and the ordered geometry shapes photon emission into a directional beam. Performance is evaluated via numerical simulations, including robustness to probabilistic atom loading, with only ten atoms required.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show single-photon collection efficiencies into a waveguide exceeding 70% through a high-NA lens, with negligible multiple excitation probability. Performance is robust against probabilistic atom loading in the standing-wave dipole traps, requiring only ten atoms.
AI.conclusion: The Rydberg quantum antenna offers a unique route toward scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, identical single-photon sources interfaced with a photonic chip, addressing key challenges in photonic quantum information technology.

title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.

AI.tldr: QECirc is an open, community-driven library that curates concrete quantum error correction circuits, making them FAIR with links to code, Stim/OpenQASM formats, visualizations, and correctness checks.
AI.motivation: QEC circuits are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but they are scattered across papers and repositories in incompatible formats, often too sparsely documented to reconstruct or reuse.
AI.method: The authors built QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven open library where each entry links to its underlying code, is provided in Stim and OpenQASM, includes interactive visualizations, and undergoes correctness checking before publication.
AI.result: QECirc makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR), complementing resources like the Error Correction Zoo by providing the concrete circuits that realize the codes.
AI.conclusion: QECirc serves as a FAIR, curated circuit repository for QEC, analogous to the Error Correction Zoo but focused on implementations rather than code descriptions.

title: Fast Unitary Preparation of Surface-Code Logical States on Neutral-Atom Hardware
summary: Preparing logical states is a constantly recurring primitive at the start of any surface-code-based quantum computation. The standard measurement-based protocol is expensive on neutral atoms, since measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, additionally require shuttling the atoms to a readout zone. In this work, we present a measurement-free, unitary preparation of surface-code Pauli eigenstates tailored to neutral atoms. A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth $(d{+}3)/2$, while retaining fault distance $d$ in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. We compile and simulate the resulting schedules with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model. The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance, and is the only construction tested that operates below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.

AI.tldr: A measurement-free, unitary scheme prepares surface-code Pauli eigenstates on neutral atoms via a bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade, compiled and simulated with bloqade under a calibrated noise model.
AI.motivation: Standard measurement-based logical state preparation is expensive on neutral atoms: measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, require shuttling atoms to a readout zone.
AI.method: A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth (d+3)/2 while retaining fault distance d in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. Schedules are compiled and simulated with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model.
AI.result: The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance and is the only tested construction operating below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measurement-free unitary preparation is the most effective tested approach for surface-code Pauli eigenstate preparation on neutral atoms, operating below threshold for both logical states.

title: Transformer fault diagnosis using an efficient simulation-driven variational quantum classifier with domain-aware feature encoding
comment: This paper has been published in Alexandria Engineering Journal. Please cite the published version
summary: Early transformer fault diagnosis is challenged by nonlinear dissolved-gas interactions, overlapping fault signatures, and limited labeled data, while practical deployment further requires reliable performance under realistic computational constraints. This paper presents a simulation-driven modeling framework for dissolved gas analysis-based transformer fault diagnosis, in which a carefully engineered variational quantum classifier (VQC) is employed as the computational core and systematically analyzed through simulation. The framework integrates domain-aware feature modeling derived from Duval geometry with a lightweight two-qubit quantum representation, enabling nonlinear gas-interaction effects to be captured within a shallow parameterized circuit. A hybrid ZX-YY quantum feature map is designed to model non-commuting feature interactions, while a full-entanglement EfficientSU2 ansatz provides adequate expressive capacity under strict resource limits. Model behavior is evaluated using a comprehensive simulation pipeline including noise-aware circuit emulation, cross-dataset validation, and limited hardware-in-the-loop execution, allowing key effects of circuit depth, noise, and optimization strategy to be examined. Simulation results on benchmark dissolved-gas-analysis datasets demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy, strong generalization capability, and robustness to realistic noise levels with minimal quantum resources. The results highlight the effectiveness of simulation-informed modeling for practical transformer diagnostic applications, offering a reproducible and resource-efficient pathway for evaluating quantum-enhanced fault diagnosis methods.

AI.tldr: A simulation-driven variational quantum classifier framework for transformer dissolved gas analysis fault diagnosis, using a two-qubit ZX-YY feature map and EfficientSU2 ansatz with Duval-geometry features, achieves high accuracy and noise robustness under minimal quantum resources.
AI.motivation: Early transformer fault diagnosis faces challenges: nonlinear dissolved-gas interactions, overlapping fault signatures, and limited labeled data. Practical deployment also requires reliable performance under realistic computational constraints, motivating a resource-efficient, simulation-informed quantum approach.
AI.method: The work develops a simulation-driven modeling framework employing a variational quantum classifier as the computational core. It integrates domain-aware feature modeling from Duval geometry with a lightweight two-qubit quantum representation. A hybrid ZX-YY quantum feature map models non-commuting feature interactions, paired with a full-entanglement EfficientSU2 ansatz for expressive capacity under strict resource limits. Evaluation uses noise-aware circuit emulation, cross-dataset validation, and limited hardware-in-the-loop execution, examining circuit depth, noise, and optimization strategy.
AI.result: Simulation results on benchmark dissolved-gas-analysis datasets show high diagnostic accuracy, strong generalization capability, and robustness to realistic noise levels while using minimal quantum resources.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-informed modeling is effective for practical transformer diagnostic applications, offering a reproducible and resource-efficient pathway for evaluating quantum-enhanced fault diagnosis methods.

title: Verification Meets Calibration: Bounds and Secret-Independent State Preparation with an NV-Center as a Case Study
summary: Verification protocols provide cryptographic guarantees that the outcome of a delegated quantum computation is correct, a key requirement for scalable and trustworthy quantum computing. A central assumption underlying these protocols is secret independence: the noise affecting state preparation must not depend on the classical secrets that specify the prepared states. In earlier protocols this assumption was enforced by the physical separation of client and server; in the recent on-chip setting it becomes a property of the hardware itself, and one that high-fidelity devices do not automatically satisfy. We first make the requirement quantitative, deriving a bound that shows how residual secret dependence limits the size of any verifiable computation within this framework. Motivated by this, we introduce a calibration framework that enforces secret independence through pulse-level quantum control, producing state preparations that are simultaneously high-fidelity and secret-independent. We assess its performance on a nitrogen-vacancy centre system via emulation, showing that it reduces the secret dependence of the preparations by more than an order of magnitude compared to standard optimal control, and that it is robust against detuning and drive-amplitude errors commonly encountered in experiment. The framework operates entirely at the calibration stage and is platform-agnostic, offering a practical pathway towards verifiable quantum computing at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the "secret independence" assumption underlying delegated quantum computation verification protocols and proposes a pulse-level calibration framework that enforces it while preserving high fidelity.
AI.motivation: Verification protocols for delegated quantum computation rely on the assumption of secret independence: the noise affecting state preparation must not depend on the classical secrets specifying the prepared states. Previously enforced by physical client-server separation, in on-chip settings this becomes a hardware property that high-fidelity devices do not automatically satisfy. The authors aim to make this requirement quantitative and to provide a practical means of enforcing it.
AI.method: The authors first derive a bound quantifying how residual secret dependence limits the size of any verifiable computation within this framework. Motivated by this bound, they introduce a calibration framework that enforces secret independence via pulse-level quantum control, yielding state preparations that are simultaneously high-fidelity and secret-independent. They evaluate it on a nitrogen-vacancy centre system through emulation.
AI.result: The calibration framework reduces the secret dependence of the preparations by more than an order of magnitude compared to standard optimal control, and it is robust against detuning and drive-amplitude errors commonly encountered in experiment.
AI.conclusion: Secret independence can be quantitatively bounded and actively enforced at the calibration stage. The framework is platform-agnostic and operates entirely during calibration, offering a practical pathway toward verifiable quantum computing at scale.

title: Phase-Flag Access and No-Go Constraints on Quotient-Space Real Quantum Mechanics
comment: This work is a follow-up to our previous study, arXiv:2607.05865
summary: Barrios Hita et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 240202 (2026)] proposed a quotient-space formulation of quantum mechanics over the real numbers and concluded that complex numbers are only a convenience. A preceding analysis [arXiv:2607.05865] showed that, when the construction is empirically equivalent to complex quantum mechanics, its real flag is protected by a hidden complex structure $\hat{J}$ and its composition rule is the balanced tensor product over that structure. Here we ask what would follow from the stronger operational reading that the flag is an accessible real degree of freedom. The answer is a direct clash with overlap-determinability (OD), introduced in [arXiv:2601.14638], and with standard no-go theorems. A readable or coherently controllable flag fixes a representative of each ray, and hence supplies precisely the phase convention that OD identifies as the missing resource for universal superposition of unknown states. Once promoted to a generic phase-access primitive, this resource enables probabilistic cloning of a linearly dependent set, steering-based signaling, and logarithmic-query unstructured search. Thus the quotient construction has a sharp follow-up interpretation: as a protected gauge representation it is standard complex quantum mechanics in real notation; as an accessible real theory it leaves the quantum operational framework.

AI.tldr: The quotient-space real formulation of quantum mechanics is either empirically equivalent to complex QM (when its real flag is gauge-protected) or, if the flag is treated as an accessible real degree of freedom, it violates overlap-determinability and standard no-go theorems, enabling probabilistic cloning, signaling, and logarithmic-query search—thus leaving the quantum operational framework.
AI.motivation: Barrios Hita et al. claimed complex numbers are merely a convenience by reformulating QM over the reals via a quotient space. This paper tests the stronger operational reading that the real flag is an accessible degree of freedom, asking whether such a reading is compatible with standard quantum operational constraints.
AI.method: Conceptual/operational analysis linking the quotient construction to overlap-determinability (OD). The flag's readability or coherent controllability is shown to fix a ray representative, supplying the phase convention OD identifies as the missing resource for universal superposition of unknown states. This resource is then promoted to a generic phase-access primitive to derive operational consequences.
AI.result: Treating the flag as accessible clashes directly with OD and standard no-go theorems. The induced phase-access resource enables probabilistic cloning of a linearly dependent set, steering-based signaling, and logarithmic-query unstructured search.
AI.conclusion: The quotient construction has a sharp dichotomy: as a protected gauge representation it is just standard complex QM in real notation; as an accessible real theory it abandons the quantum operational framework. Complex numbers are therefore not a mere convenience in any operationally meaningful reading.

title: Bandwidth-Tunable Quantum Light Source at 1.5 $μ$m
summary: Quantum light sources constitute a crucial physical resource for the construction of quantum networks. Despite remarkable recent progress, there remains a lack of systematic investigation into the bandwidth tunability of quantum light sources under fixed waveguide parameters. In this work, we demonstrate a broadband quantum light source in the 1.5 $μ$m band with tunable bandwidth by changing the temperature of a piece of periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide. In our demonstration, the bandwidth of the quantum light source is tuned from 78.3 nm to 96.2 nm with a temperature change of 1 $^\circ$C . Under different bandwidths, the generation rates of correlated photon pairs are greater than 6.3 MHz with coincidence-to-accidental ratios consistently being no less than 608. The energy-time entanglement properties are measured by using the Franson interference with two-photon interference visibilities larger than 99.06%. Our results provide an effective method for developing the quantum light sources with tunable bandwidth which has great potential for building the large-scale quantum networks.

AI.tldr: A broadband 1.5 μm quantum light source with temperature-tunable bandwidth is demonstrated in a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide, showing high pair generation rates, excellent coincidence-to-accidental ratios, and strong energy-time entanglement.
AI.motivation: Quantum light sources are essential for quantum networks, but the bandwidth tunability of such sources under fixed waveguide parameters has not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors vary the temperature of a periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) waveguide to tune the bandwidth of a 1.5 μm band quantum light source, and characterize correlated photon pair generation and energy-time entanglement via Franson interference.
AI.result: Bandwidth is tuned from 78.3 nm to 96.2 nm with a 1 °C temperature change; correlated photon pair generation rates exceed 6.3 MHz, coincidence-to-accidental ratios are no less than 608, and two-photon interference visibilities exceed 99.06%.
AI.conclusion: Temperature tuning of a PPLN waveguide offers an effective method for realizing quantum light sources with tunable bandwidth, promising for large-scale quantum networks.

title: Quantum Speedups for Log-Concave Sampling from Local Structure
summary: For a convex function $f \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, the problem of sampling from a distribution proportional to $e^{-f(x)}$ is called log-concave sampling. In many practical scenarios, the function $f(x)$ turns out to admit a local decomposition $f(x) = \sum_{a=1}^R ψ_a(x_{S_a})$. In this paper, we consider log-concave sampling using local queries, i.e., evaluation and gradient queries to each clause $ψ_a(\cdot)$, which can be computationally much cheaper than the queries to $f(x)$ itself. We show that if each coordinate appears in only a small number of clauses, there is a quantum algorithm for strongly log-concave sampling using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrtκd)$ local queries, where $κ$ is the condition number. This improves the prior best classical result $\widetilde{O}(κd)$ due to Ascolani, Lavenant, and Zanella (Ann. Probab. 2026) and the quantum result $\widetilde{O}(\sqrtκ d^2)$ implied by Childs et al. (NeurIPS 2022). Our quantum sampler applies to a broad class of locally structured models from statistical computing and machine learning, with representative examples including Gaussian Markov random fields, finite-element latent Gaussian models, and sparse generalized linear models. These results demonstrate that local structure is not merely an implementation detail, but a quantum algorithmic resource for high-dimensional sampling.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm samples from strongly log-concave distributions with locally decomposable f using Õ(√κ d) local queries, improving prior classical Õ(κd) and quantum Õ(√κ d²) bounds.
AI.motivation: In practice f(x) often decomposes as a sum of local clause functions ψ_a(x_{S_a}), and querying each ψ_a is far cheaper than querying f itself. The paper asks whether this local structure can be exploited algorithmically, and specifically whether quantum methods can outperform the best classical sampler for this setting.
AI.method: The authors design a quantum log-concave sampling algorithm that uses local queries (evaluation and gradient queries to individual clauses ψ_a) rather than queries to the full function f. The analysis assumes strong log-concavity and bounded coordinate participation (each coordinate appears in only a small number of clauses), with complexity measured in local queries as a function of the condition number κ and dimension d.
AI.result: The sampler achieves Õ(√κ d) local queries, improving on the prior best classical bound Õ(κd) (Ascolani, Lavenant, Zanella, Ann. Probab. 2026) and the quantum bound Õ(√κ d²) implied by Childs et al. (NeurIPS 2022). It applies to Gaussian Markov random fields, finite-element latent Gaussian models, and sparse generalized linear models.
AI.conclusion: Local structure is not merely an implementation detail but a genuine quantum algorithmic resource for high-dimensional sampling.

title: Multiparameter sensing of axion dark matter with superconducting-qubit networks
summary: We propose a quantum sensor network for direct detection of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion dark matter using entangled superconducting qubits. In the presence of a static magnetic field, the oscillating axion field induces a coherent qubit rotation described by an encoding angle proportional to the axion-photon coupling and an unknown dark-matter phase. Treating the phase as an additional unknown parameter turns axion detection into a two-parameter quantum estimation problem. We formulate these signals in Cartesian coordinates, thereby avoiding the singularity that arises in the weak-signal regime and establishing a regular framework for multiparameter quantum estimation. Using this framework, we optimize the quantum sensor network and combine it with Bayesian inference to reconstruct the axion-photon coupling. The optimized protocol accurately recovers the KSVZ and DFSZ benchmark couplings over the mass range $m_a\in[0.1,10]~μ{\rm eV}$, generalizes to previously unseen masses, and remains robust against realistic superconducting-qubit decoherence and gate errors.
