AI.tldr: A quantum sensor network of entangled superconducting qubits is proposed for direct detection of QCD axion dark matter, formulated as a two-parameter quantum estimation problem and combined with Bayesian inference.
AI.motivation: Direct detection of QCD axion dark matter is challenging. The oscillating axion field in a static magnetic field induces a coherent qubit rotation with an encoding angle proportional to the axion-photon coupling, but an unknown dark-matter phase complicates the estimation, especially in the weak-signal regime where singularities arise.
AI.method: The phase is treated as an additional unknown parameter, turning axion detection into a two-parameter quantum estimation problem. Signals are formulated in Cartesian coordinates to avoid the weak-signal singularity and establish a regular multiparameter quantum estimation framework. The quantum sensor network is then optimized and combined with Bayesian inference to reconstruct the axion-photon coupling.
AI.result: The optimized protocol accurately recovers the KSVZ and DFSZ benchmark couplings over the mass range m_a in [0.1, 10] μeV, generalizes to previously unseen masses, and remains robust against realistic superconducting-qubit decoherence and gate errors.
AI.conclusion: Entangled superconducting-qubit sensor networks with a Cartesian-coordinate multiparameter estimation framework and Bayesian inference enable robust, accurate reconstruction of axion-photon couplings across a broad mass range.

title: A Protocol-Guided LLM Agent for Quantum Program Synthesis and Execution
summary: This study evaluates a protocol-guided large language model (LLM) agent workflow for quantum program synthesis and execution. A versioned YAML protocol specifies interface and quantum-semantic requirements while leaving circuit design to the model. The workflow combines Qiskit circuit generation, evaluator-guided repair, and quantum processing unit (QPU) deployment. A matched ablation evaluates four LLM endpoints using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for H$_2$, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut, and Fashion-MNIST quantum-kernel classification. Across 240 trials, protocol guidance increased evaluator completion from 80.0\% to 99.2\%, reduced mean repairs from 2.56 to 0.75, and reduced mean agent time from 55.70 to 30.58~s. Provider-reported token use decreased for three of four endpoints. Completed VQE trials meeting chemical accuracy increased from 16/40 to 29/40, while valid QAOA approximation ratios remained comparable. Semantic review identified rank-one fidelity kernels, reinforcing the distinction between evaluator completion and semantic validity. A 210-run IBM QPU study evaluated the combined generation-and-selection pipelines and confirmed deployment feasibility. The results support protocol guidance as a software-reliability layer that must be complemented by quantum-semantic validation.

AI.tldr: A versioned YAML protocol guiding an LLM agent workflow for quantum program synthesis improves evaluator completion (80.0%→99.2%), cuts repairs (2.56→0.75) and agent time (55.70s→30.58s), and raises chemically accurate VQE results (16/40→29/40), while QAOA ratios stay comparable; semantic review still flags invalid kernels, and a 210-run IBM QPU study confirms deployment feasibility.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can generate quantum programs, but raw model outputs are unreliable: many candidates fail interface or quantum-semantic requirements, requiring costly repair loops. The paper asks whether constraining the agent with an explicit protocol improves software reliability without over-specifying circuit design, and whether such guidance alone guarantees semantic validity.
AI.method: A versioned YAML protocol encodes interface and quantum-semantic requirements while leaving circuit design to the model. The workflow comprises Qiskit circuit generation, evaluator-guided repair, and QPU deployment. A matched ablation compares four LLM endpoints across three tasks—VQE for H2, QAOA for MaxCut, and Fashion-MNIST quantum-kernel classification—over 240 trials, plus a 210-run IBM QPU study of combined generation-and-selection pipelines.
AI.result: Protocol guidance raised evaluator completion from 80.0% to 99.2%, reduced mean repairs from 2.56 to 0.75, and cut mean agent time from 55.70 s to 30.58 s; token use fell for three of four endpoints. Chemically accurate VQE trials rose from 16/40 to 29/40, while valid QAOA approximation ratios remained comparable. Semantic review exposed rank-one fidelity kernels, and the IBM QPU study confirmed deployment feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Protocol guidance acts as a software-reliability layer for LLM-driven quantum program synthesis, improving completion, efficiency, and numerical quality. However, it does not ensure quantum-semantic validity, so it must be complemented by dedicated semantic validation before deployment.

title: QEncodeBench: Can Large Language Models Encode Classical Problems into Verified Quantum Oracles?
summary: Grover search, amplitude amplification, and quantum counting all rely on the same reusable subroutine, a phase oracle, whose construction the algorithms literature takes as given: the classical predicate is assumed to be already encoded as a correct, resource-bounded circuit. We turn this assumption into a measured capability. QEncodeBench tasks large language models (LLMs) with encoding classical constraint problems as phase oracles and scores the generated circuits with an adversarially self-validated verifier that decides full solution-set equivalence up to a global phase, with ancillas restored and resource budgets enforced. Sampled basis-state tests, we show, systematically overestimate this ability. Measured this way, models separate sharply: code models without a reasoning mode solve essentially nothing, and enabling native reasoning on identical weights improves accuracy by an order of magnitude. The failures are overwhelmingly semantic rather than syntactic. Two architectures, a unit-verified constraint agent and a neuro-symbolic compilation pipeline, close most of the remaining gap by delegating correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures. Ablations quantify the contribution of each component, and resource gating exposes an architecture-dependent trade-off between circuit width and depth. Finally, controlled difficulty escalation reveals architecture-specific responses to difficulty structure: different difficulty axes degrade different methods, while the neuro-symbolic pipeline passes every evaluated instance. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chexujun/QEncodeBench.

AI.tldr: QEncodeBench benchmarks LLMs on encoding classical constraint problems into quantum phase oracles, using an adversarially self-validated verifier that checks full solution-set equivalence up to global phase; it shows sampled basis-state tests overestimate ability, reasoning mode yields ~10x accuracy gains, and two architectures (constraint agent, neuro-symbolic pipeline) largely close the gap.
AI.motivation: Grover search, amplitude amplification, and quantum counting all depend on a reusable phase oracle subroutine, but the algorithms literature assumes this oracle is already given as a correct, resource-bounded circuit. The paper challenges this assumption by treating phase-oracle construction as a measured capability of LLMs.
AI.method: QEncodeBench tasks LLMs with encoding classical constraint problems as phase oracles. Generated circuits are scored by an adversarially self-validated verifier that decides full solution-set equivalence up to a global phase, with ancillas restored and resource budgets enforced. The authors compare against sampled basis-state testing, test reasoning vs. non-reasoning code models, and evaluate two architectures: a unit-verified constraint agent and a neuro-symbolic compilation pipeline. Ablations and resource gating isolate component contributions and width/depth trade-offs, and controlled difficulty escalation probes architecture-specific responses.
AI.result: Sampled basis-state tests systematically overestimate phase-oracle encoding ability. Code models without a reasoning mode solve essentially nothing; enabling native reasoning on identical weights improves accuracy by an order of magnitude. Failures are overwhelmingly semantic rather than syntactic. The unit-verified constraint agent and the neuro-symbolic compilation pipeline close most of the remaining gap by delegating correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures. Resource gating exposes an architecture-dependent circuit width vs. depth trade-off, and difficulty escalation degrades different methods along different axes, while the neuro-symbolic pipeline passes every evaluated instance.
AI.conclusion: Phase-oracle construction should be treated as an empirically measurable LLM capability rather than a given. Rigorous equivalence-based verification reveals that weak testing inflates perceived ability, reasoning mode is critical, and the dominant failure mode is semantic. Delegating correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures (as in the neuro-symbolic pipeline) is the most robust strategy, achieving full pass rates under escalating difficulty. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chexujun/QEncodeBench.

title: Divergence Geometry of Quantum Multi-Mpemba Effects
summary: Whether a quantum Mpemba effect occurs can depend on how distance from stationarity is measured. We show that agreement across normalized operator-convex Petz divergences is decided by a one-parameter $χ^2$ profile. Its sign fixes the common order, alternating sign margins guarantee repeated crossings, and finite dimension yields a polynomial positivity test. The same profile explains diagnostic-independent late-time order for a simple real slow mode and isolates coherence as the local source of diagnostic dependence. In a trapped-ion qutrit ideal model, the reported preparation gives diagnostic-selective crossings, while a nearby preparation is a floating-point candidate for two family-wide reversals. The framework turns diagnostic robustness into a tractable control problem.

AI.tldr: Whether a quantum Mpemba effect occurs depends on the distance measure used; agreement across normalized operator-convex Petz divergences is governed by a one-parameter chi-squared profile, enabling a polynomial positivity test for crossings and framing diagnostic robustness as a control problem.
AI.motivation: The existence of a quantum Mpemba effect can be diagnostic-dependent, i.e., it may appear or vanish depending on how distance from stationarity is quantified. This ambiguity calls for a unifying characterization of when different divergences agree or disagree on the order of relaxation.
AI.method: The authors analyze normalized operator-convex Petz divergences and show that their agreement is determined by a one-parameter chi-squared profile. The sign of this profile fixes the common order, alternating-sign margins guarantee repeated crossings, and finite dimensionality reduces the problem to a polynomial positivity test. They further connect the profile to a simple real slow mode and identify coherence as the local source of diagnostic dependence, illustrating with a trapped-ion qutrit ideal model.
AI.result: A single one-parameter chi-squared profile decides agreement across the divergence family, with its sign setting the shared ordering and alternating-sign margins producing repeated crossings. The framework yields a polynomial positivity test in finite dimensions, explains diagnostic-independent late-time order via a simple real slow mode, isolates coherence as the local origin of diagnostic dependence, and in a trapped-ion qutrit model identifies a preparation giving diagnostic-selective crossings plus a nearby floating-point candidate for two family-wide reversals.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic robustness of the quantum Mpemba effect can be systematically characterized and controlled through the chi-squared profile, turning the question of measure-independent behavior into a tractable control problem.

title: Dissipative phase transitions in quantum reservoir computing
summary: Enhanced performance of quantum reservoir computing has been associated with dynamical phase transitions, but whether this connection extends to dissipative systems and which relaxation mechanisms underlie it remain insufficiently understood. We systematically compare driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions and find enhanced memory and nonlinear processing near both phase boundaries. Although the closure of the Liouvillian gap marks the transitions in the thermodynamic limit, computational performance does not generally follow gap suppression. An exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition quantitatively attributes the trained memory to intrinsic relaxation channels. It shows that the gap mode contributes only weakly, while finite-rate modes and their cross-contributions dominate the enhanced capacity. These results go beyond phenomenological correlations by directly linking memory capacity to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum. Moreover, these findings provide a physical basis for designing dissipative quantum reservoirs and testing memory-enhancement mechanisms in experimentally accessible Kerr platforms.

AI.tldr: Enhanced quantum reservoir computing near dissipative phase transitions is driven not by the Liouvillian gap mode but by finite-rate relaxation modes and their cross-contributions, revealed via an exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition.
AI.motivation: Prior work links enhanced quantum reservoir computing performance to dynamical phase transitions, but it is unclear whether this connection holds in dissipative systems and which relaxation mechanisms are responsible. This gap motivates a systematic study of driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across different phase transition types.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions, evaluating memory and nonlinear processing. They apply an exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition to attribute trained memory to specific intrinsic relaxation channels.
AI.result: Enhanced memory and nonlinear processing occur near both phase boundaries. Although the Liouvillian gap closes at the transitions in the thermodynamic limit, computational performance does not generally track gap suppression. The decomposition shows the gap mode contributes only weakly, while finite-rate modes and their cross-contributions dominate the enhanced capacity.
AI.conclusion: The work moves beyond phenomenological correlations by directly linking memory capacity to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum, offering a physical basis for designing dissipative quantum reservoirs and testing memory-enhancement mechanisms in experimentally accessible Kerr platforms.

title: Entanglement Dynamics in Katz-Weighted Graph States
summary:
We investigate the entanglement dynamics of quantum states defined on graphs with non-local Ising interactions governed by the Katz kernel of the underlying network. The interaction pattern is physically motivated by a gapped fermionic mediator propagating on the same graph, whose perturbative elimination yields an effective Katz-weighted Ising Hamiltonian. Using the Entanglement Distance, we derive an exact analytical expression for the entanglement generated from an initially separable state and apply it to representative deterministic graph families.
  We then characterize the dynamics in different propagation regimes. In the weak-Katz regime, the dynamics admits a systematic motif expansion with triangles entering at first order order and four-cycles, local degree structure, and overlappin triangles appearing at second order. In the strong-propagation regime, the interaction is instead dominated by the principal adjacency mode and by the localization properties of its eigenvector. For Erdős--Rényi graphs, the weak-propagation expansion can be averaged analytically, revealing a locally tree-like contribution in the sparse regime and saturation of the Entanglement Distance density in the dense regime.
  Our results connect entanglement dynamics with both the walk-based and spectral structure of complex networks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entanglement dynamics for quantum states on graphs with non-local Ising interactions weighted by the Katz kernel, motivated by a fermionic mediator on the same graph. Using the Entanglement Distance, the authors derive an exact analytical expression for entanglement generated from a separable state, analyze weak- and strong-propagation regimes, and analytically average the weak regime for Erdős–Rényi graphs, linking entanglement to walk-based and spectral network structure.
AI.motivation: Understanding how complex network topology governs entanglement generation is a central question at the interface of quantum information and network science. The authors seek a physically grounded interaction model that connects graph structure—both its walk-based and spectral properties—to entanglement dynamics, using a perturbatively derived Katz-weighted Ising Hamiltonian.
AI.method: A gapped fermionic mediator propagating on the graph is perturbatively eliminated to yield an effective non-local Ising Hamiltonian weighted by the Katz kernel. Entanglement generated from an initially separable state is quantified via the Entanglement Distance, for which an exact analytical expression is derived. The dynamics are then characterized through a weak-Katz regime (systematic motif expansion) and a strong-propagation regime (principal adjacency mode and eigenvector localization), with analytical averaging over Erdős–Rényi ensembles.
AI.result: An exact analytical expression for the entanglement generated from a separable state is obtained and applied to representative deterministic graph families. In the weak-Katz regime, triangles appear at first order, while four-cycles, local degree structure, and overlapping triangles enter at second order. In the strong-propagation regime, interactions are dominated by the principal adjacency mode and its eigenvector localization. For Erdős–Rényi graphs, the averaged weak expansion yields a locally tree-like contribution in the sparse regime and saturation of the Entanglement Distance density in the dense regime.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement dynamics under Katz-weighted Ising interactions is jointly governed by the walk-based and spectral structure of complex networks, providing a unified bridge between network topology and quantum entanglement generation.

title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
summary: Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes how the measurement (shot-noise) resource overhead scales with system size when simulating NMR spectra on quantum computers, finding only weak (sub-exponential) growth, suggesting shot noise is not a fundamental barrier to quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing hardware advances motivate finding applications showing quantum advantage; simulating quantum many-body systems is promising because classical resources grow exponentially with system size (due to Hilbert space growth). However, digital quantum computers do not output deterministic results—projective measurements are affected by shot noise, and expectation values must be reconstructed from repeated measurements. The number of measurements is thus a key computational resource that must be assessed before claiming quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors study how the measurement resource scales with system size, where the scaling itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result. They use NMR spectral simulation as a test case, examining both real-world molecules and a class of model NMR Hamiltonians enabling efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interaction geometries.
AI.result: The required resources (number of measurements/shots) increase only weakly with molecular size, remaining far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space.
AI.conclusion: Shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

title: State-Selective Floquet Memory in Degenerate Manifolds
summary: In order to understand which initial states retain memory under periodic driving, it is necessary to depart from the ideal limit giving rise to invariant structures and work inside near-degenerate manifolds. We show that degeneracy itself is not conclusive and what actually matters is how perturbations, such as structural and driving imperfections, acts on the projected multiplet. For systems decoupling into the local clusters in the ideal limit, the projections can be computed within degenerate perturbation theory. There the stability is decided by two criteria: the coupling can not connect the state with other degenerate partners in the manifold, either by kinetic blocking, or more generally, by diagonalizing the projected coupling, and the drive's local selection rule must admit only transfer energies detuned from Floquet sidebands, in which case the projected drive generator exactly vanishes. We formalize these understandings in a periodically driven clean, short-ranged alternating XXZ chain and demonstrate a set of results that include, long-lived states, both of product form and entangled across the clusters, a periodic family of sideband resonances, and an explicit example showing opposite fates for states with identical energy and charges.

AI.tldr: Memory retention under periodic driving is governed not by degeneracy per se, but by how perturbations act on the projected multiplet: stability requires either kinetic blocking/diagonalization of the projected coupling and a drive selection rule admitting only Floquet-sideband-detuned transfer energies.
AI.motivation: To understand which initial states retain memory under periodic driving, one must leave the ideal limit that produces invariant structures and work inside near-degenerate manifolds, where the role of perturbations (structural and driving imperfections) remains unclear.
AI.method: Degenerate perturbation theory is used to compute projections for systems decoupling into local clusters in the ideal limit. Two stability criteria are established: (i) the coupling must not connect a state to other degenerate partners in the manifold, either via kinetic blocking or by diagonalizing the projected coupling; (ii) the drive's local selection rule must admit only transfer energies detuned from Floquet sidebands, making the projected drive generator vanish exactly. These ideas are formalized in a periodically driven clean, short-ranged alternating XXZ chain.
AI.result: The framework yields long-lived states of both product form and entangled across clusters, a periodic family of sideband resonances, and an explicit example showing opposite fates for states with identical energy and charges.
AI.conclusion: Degeneracy alone is not conclusive for memory retention; what matters is how perturbations act on the projected multiplet, as captured by the two proposed criteria.

title: VQE Validation on the Mononuclear T1 (Blue-Copper) Site: A Stepping Stone to the Multi-Copper Laccase Cluster
summary: Validating variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) pipelines on realistic chemical systems is a critical stepping stone toward tackling classically intractable molecules. In this work, we report emulator-based validation of the VQE workflow proposed for the copper active site, executed on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator. A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE with a full singles-doubles-triples (S+D+T) pool removes over 99% of the correlation error, reaching a stable plateau at 4.03 mEh relative to exact diagonalisation (148 selected operators). This establishes a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA). Finally, we frame these emulator results as a robust baseline for upcoming physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.

AI.tldr: Emulator-based validation of an ADAPT-VQE pipeline for the copper active site on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator, with a full singles-doubles-triples pool reaching 4.03 mEh from exact diagonalisation and >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz.
AI.motivation: Validating VQE pipelines on realistic chemical systems is a critical stepping stone toward tackling classically intractable molecules; this work targets the copper active site as such a realistic test case.
AI.method: A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE using a full singles-doubles-triples (S+D+T) operator pool, executed on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator.
AI.result: The approach removes over 99% of the correlation error, reaching a stable plateau at 4.03 mEh relative to exact diagonalisation with 148 selected operators, and achieves a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA).
AI.conclusion: The emulator results serve as a robust baseline for upcoming physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.

title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
summary: Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.

AI.tldr: Neutral atom arrays are versatile platforms for digital and analogue quantum computing/simulation, with capabilities spanning large-scale programmable Hamiltonians and error-corrected logical qubits, and are reviewed here for their relevance to materials science and quantum chemistry.
AI.motivation: The abstract highlights that neutral atom arrays have matured as platforms for both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, but a consolidated overview connecting this hardware to applications in materials science and quantum chemistry is needed.
AI.method: Review/overview approach (no primary experimental method disclosed in the abstract).
AI.result: Reported demonstrations include large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realizing topological phases, weighted graph optimisation, and error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a broad overview of the neutral atom platform and its potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.

title: Noise-Robust Quantum State Characterization for Remote State Preparation with Deep Learning
summary: Quantum communication underpins secure information processing and scalable quantum networks. In particular, remote state preparation (RSP) enables efficient quantum state transfer, but accurately estimating target states under complex noise remains challenging. Here, we propose a Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) model for noisy RSP experiments. Our model reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy measurements in complex scattering environments, while its attention patterns provide physically grounded insights into correlations among the measured observables. The method achieves a mean estimator-target fidelity exceeding 99.999% under complex scattering and dynamic Gaussian noise, while its robustness and generalization are further examined using Qiskit-simulated Bloch-ball states.Furthermore, in a practical MNIST image transmission task with held-out states, the decoded bit error rate is reduced from 50.34% to zero after TQSC post-processing. The TQSC model enables accurate tomographic characterization under dynamic noise and provides physically grounded post-hoc insights, holding promise for intelligent quantum information processing applications.

AI.method: A Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) model is developed. It reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy measurements in complex scattering environments, and its attention patterns are analyzed to extract physically grounded correlations among measured observables. Robustness and generalization are tested with Qiskit-simulated Bloch-ball states.

title: Coherent error threshold for quantum LDPC codes
summary: A key appeal of quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes is their ability to suppress stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds. Coherent errors are fundamentally different: they produce superpositions of error patterns whose amplitudes can interfere even after syndrome measurement. Rigorous understanding of coherent errors remains limited. Here we show that general qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code capacity threshold against local coherent noise and more generally local channel noise. For any family of qLDPC codes with distance $d=Ω(\log n)$, we show that there is a constant noise strength below which the logical recovery error in diamond distance decays exponentially with the code distance. The result is established for optimal recovery as well as the minimum-weight decoder. The key technical ingredient is what we call a \emph{cluster resummation}: rather than bounding superposed error configurations one by one, we isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms. Standard cluster counting then yields exponential suppression. This work resolves a longstanding challenge in fault tolerance theory, providing general robustness guarantees for qLDPC codes against coherent noise and laying a rigorous foundation for future studies of fault-tolerant quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: General qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code-capacity threshold against local coherent (and more generally local channel) noise: for distance d=Ω(log n), optimal and minimum-weight recovery achieve logical error in diamond distance decaying exponentially with d below a constant noise strength, proven via a novel "cluster resummation" technique.
AI.motivation: qLDPC codes are prized for suppressing stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds, but coherent errors behave fundamentally differently—producing superposed error patterns whose amplitudes interfere even after syndrome measurement—and rigorous understanding of coherent errors remains limited. The paper addresses this longstanding challenge in fault-tolerance theory.

The key technical ingredient is "cluster resummation": instead of bounding superposed error configurations individually, they isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms, then apply standard cluster counting to obtain exponential suppression.

title: Technical Report OFDM-Assisted Simultaneous Quantum and Classical THz Communications
summary: The feasibility of cost-effective simultaneous quantum and classical communication (SQCC) transmitting both the quantum key and classical information via a superimposed coherent state is investigated both in optical and Terahertz (THz) bands. Since the existing THz SQCC schemes assume single-carrier (SC) transmission over flat fading channels, we embark on investigating SQCC in realistic frequency-selective multipath THz fading channels. We then propose an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) based SQCC system for time-invariant frequency-selective THz scenarios, supported by low-density parity-check coded (LDPC) multidimensional QKD reconciliation schemes. Our simulation results demonstrate that the OFDM-based SQCC scheme is capable of achieving a practical secret key rate (SKR) over a wide range of power sharing scenarios between the classical and quantum signals. By contrast its single-carrier counterpart requires the classical signal to be at least 100 times stronger than the quantum signal in THz SQCC.

AI.tldr: This paper studies cost-effective simultaneous quantum and classical communication (SQCC) over optical and THz bands, proposing an OFDM-based SQCC scheme for realistic frequency-selective multipath THz channels with LDPC-coded multidimensional QKD reconciliation, achieving practical secret key rates across wide power-sharing ranges.
AI.motivation: Existing THz SQCC schemes assume single-carrier transmission over flat fading channels, which is unrealistic. Real THz channels exhibit frequency-selective multipath fading, degrading SQCC performance and limiting practical secret key rates.
AI.method: The paper investigates SQCC feasibility in both optical and THz bands, transmitting quantum keys and classical information via superimposed coherent states. It analyzes realistic frequency-selective multipath THz fading channels and proposes an OFDM-based SQCC system for time-invariant frequency-selective THz scenarios, supported by low-density parity-check (LDPC) coded multidimensional QKD reconciliation schemes.

In contrast, the single-carrier counterpart requires the classical signal to be at least 100 times stronger than the quantum signal in THz SQCC.
AI.conclusion: OFDM-based SQCC with LDPC-coded multidimensional reconciliation is a viable approach for cost-effective simultaneous quantum and classical communication in realistic frequency-selective THz channels, offering a practical SKR and relaxing the stringent power-sharing constraints of single-carrier SQCC.

title: Scalable logical qubits
summary: Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of "scalable logical qubits" to make progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable, and characterizes them along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
AI.motivation: Utility-scale quantum computing requires executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can directly support, necessitating error-corrected logical qubits. However, there is a lack of a common definition to make progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable.
AI.method: The paper defines scalable logical qubits as logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands as required by applications. These scalable logical qubits are characterized along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
AI.result: The paper characterizes scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions (reliability, scale, capability, and performance) and discusses the trade-offs among these dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The definition of scalable logical qubits provides a framework to measure and compare progress toward utility-scale quantum computing, highlighting the coupled dimensions and trade-offs that must be considered.

title: FT-Weave: Real-Time Compilation Framework for Reconfigurable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Architectures
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) is essential for large-scale quantum computation, but realizing useful application throughput requires coordinating resource preparation, assignment, routing, and logical execution under strict hardware and timing constraints. Many FTQC compilation approaches construct offline schedules using nominal or fixed magic-state factory throughput. Such schedules cannot respond to stochastic resource-preparation and teleportation outcomes, leading to execution stalls and hardware underutilization. In this work, we introduce FT-Weave, a stage-aware real-time FTQC compilation framework that jointly coordinates resource preparation, resource assignment, teleportation routing, and correction handling. By adapting to runtime resource availability and hardware constraints, FT-Weave allows preparation, communication, and logical execution to overlap. We instantiate FT-Weave on two representative neutral-atom, early FTQC architectures: transversal STAR and a T-state cultivation architecture. Under the evaluated hardware and latency model, FT-Weave achieves a speedup of up to 3X over a baseline compilation flow for simulations of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. In the case study, we further find that maximizing exposed concurrency does not necessarily minimize execution time. Although fine-grained asynchronous execution can reduce local idle time, its smaller optimization windows and increased routing contention can outweigh these gains. Together, these results show that effective runtime coordination, rather then exposed parallelism alone, determines how efficiently FTQC resources translate into application throughput:FT-Weave provides a blueprint for solving this real-time orchestration problem across resource protocols and architectures.

AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires coordinating resource preparation, assignment, routing, and logical execution under strict hardware and timing constraints. Existing FTQC compilation approaches often construct offline schedules using nominal or fixed magic-state factory throughput, which cannot respond to stochastic resource-preparation and teleportation outcomes, causing execution stalls and hardware underutilization.

It adapts to runtime resource availability and hardware constraints, allowing preparation, communication, and logical execution to overlap. FT-Weave is instantiated on two representative neutral-atom, early FTQC architectures: transversal STAR and a T-state cultivation architecture.
