title: Experimental demonstration of finite-size general security via discrete-modulated CVQKD with real time postprocessing
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) is compatible with telecommunication infrastructure, but implementing composable security with experimentally practical resources has remained challenging, particularly for discrete-modulated (DM) protocols. We report the first experimental demonstration of a DM CVQKD system that generates composable secret keys against general attacks with finite-size block lengths on the order of $\sim 10^{6}$ rounds via a quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK) system. Our implementation follows a variable-length, general security framework enabled by modern entropy accumulation techniques and conic optimization, whose experimental pipeline allows real-time operation on near-commercial hardware.

AI.tldr: First experimental demonstration of a discrete-modulated CVQKD system generating composable secret keys against general attacks with finite-size block lengths (~10^6 rounds) using QPSK, enabled by entropy accumulation and conic optimization on near-commercial hardware.
AI.motivation: CVQKD is compatible with telecom infrastructure, but achieving composable security with practical resources has been difficult, especially for discrete-modulated (DM) protocols. A gap exists between theoretical security frameworks and experimentally practical, real-time implementations.
AI.method: A QPSK-based DM CVQKD implementation following a variable-length, general security framework. Security is established via modern entropy accumulation techniques combined with conic optimization, with an experimental pipeline enabling real-time operation on near-commercial hardware.
AI.result: Composable secret keys were generated against general attacks at finite-size block lengths on the order of ~10^6 rounds.
AI.conclusion: Practical, composably secure DM CVQKD is experimentally feasible with realistic block sizes and near-commercial hardware, bridging theory and deployment for telecom-compatible quantum key distribution.

title: Proof of Shor's conjecture on the accessible information of quantum dichotomies
summary: The accessible information of any given quantum ensemble quantifies the maximum amount of Shannon information that can be extracted from the ensemble by any quantum measurement. Almost three decades ago, Shor conjectured that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy, that is, an ensemble of two states, is attained by a projective measurement. Recently, a proof of this conjecture restricted to the qubit case was published by Keil. Here, we conclusively settle this longstanding open problem. First, we show that Shor's conjecture follows, in arbitrary dimension, from a recent result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, and we provide a self-contained, elementary proof. Second, for any given dichotomy and measurement, we provide the explicit construction of a projective measurement that outperforms such a measurement in extracting information from the given dichotomy. Third, while the computation of the accessible information is known to be non-convex in general, we frame the computation of the accessible information of dihotomies as a convex problem.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves Shor's three-decade-old conjecture by proving that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy (an ensemble of two states) is attained by a projective measurement, in arbitrary dimension.
AI.motivation: Shor conjectured nearly thirty years ago that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy is achieved by a projective measurement. Prior to this work, only a restricted proof for the qubit case (by Keil) existed, leaving the general problem open.
AI.method: The authors first show that Shor's conjecture, in arbitrary dimension, follows from a recent result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, and supply a self-contained elementary proof. Additionally, for any given dichotomy and measurement, they explicitly construct a projective measurement that outperforms the given measurement in extracting information. They also reformulate the computation of accessible information for dichotomies as a convex problem.
AI.result: The longstanding Shor conjecture is conclusively settled in arbitrary dimension. An explicit projective measurement is constructed that outperforms any given measurement for a dichotomy. The computation of accessible information for dichotomies is recast as a convex problem, despite the general non-convexity of accessible information computation.
AI.conclusion: Shor's conjecture holds in arbitrary dimension, and the accessible information of dichotomies admits both an optimal projective measurement construction and a convex computational formulation, fully resolving the open problem.

title: Quantum Noise Limited Nonlinear Phase-Preserving Amplification of a Bosonic Mode
summary: Does quantum mechanics allow for deterministic amplification schemes that simultaneously behave uniformly for all angles of bosonic phase space (i.e. phase preserving) and are nonlinear in the underlying field operators? Would such a scheme have some utility to quantum information science? In this paper we answer both questions with a resounding yes. Such amplifiers exist, but their form is highly constrained compared to the more general set of noise limited nonlinear amplifiers previously studied in the literature. This enables us to characterize the entire class of bosonic noise-limited nonlinear phase preserving amplifiers, and identify their utility: namely, the optimal amplification of Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.

AI.tldr: The paper affirms the existence of nonlinear, phase-preserving, noise-limited bosonic amplifiers that behave uniformly across all phase-space angles, characterizes the entire class of such amplifiers, and shows they optimally amplify Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.
AI.motivation: The authors ask whether quantum mechanics permits deterministic amplification that is simultaneously phase preserving (uniform across all bosonic phase-space angles) and nonlinear in the field operators, and whether such a scheme would be useful to quantum information science.
AI.method: The authors analyze the constraints imposed by requiring phase preservation together with nonlinearity under noise-limited operation, which is more restrictive than general noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers previously studied, and use this to characterize the full class of such amplifiers.
AI.result: Such amplifiers do exist, but their form is highly constrained relative to previously studied noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers; the entire class of bosonic noise-limited nonlinear phase-preserving amplifiers is characterized.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear, phase-preserving, noise-limited bosonic amplifiers exist and are useful, notably for the optimal amplification of Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.

title: Hardness of Pathfinding in a Welded Tree
summary:
Starting from the entrance of a welded tree, a quantum walk algorithm can find its exit vertex exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, it has been an open question whether any quantum algorithm is able to efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. We answer this by proving an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding such path. Specifically, for trees of height $n$, any quantum query algorithm requires at least $Ω(2^{n/24})$ queries in order to succeed with constant probability.
  Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle technique in order to construct databases which track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, and show that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.

AI.tldr: This paper proves an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding an entrance-to-exit path in a welded tree, showing no efficient quantum algorithm can achieve this.
AI.motivation: Quantum walks can find the exit of a welded tree exponentially faster than classical algorithms, but whether a quantum algorithm can efficiently find an actual path from entrance to exit remained open. This paper addresses that gap.
AI.method: The authors use the compressed permutation oracle technique to construct databases that track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, then show no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.
AI.result: For trees of height n, any quantum query algorithm requires at least Ω(2^{n/24}) queries to succeed with constant probability.
AI.conclusion: Finding an entrance-to-exit path in a welded tree requires exponentially many quantum queries, establishing a lower bound that matches the difficulty of the path-finding problem.

title: Multinegativity and single-letter formulas for asymptotic entanglement
summary: The study of entanglement inevitably leads to the concept of regularization, where measures are evaluated on infinitely many copies of a state. Single-letter formulas try to make these asymptotic entanglement quantities accessible through a calculation on one copy of a state, but are rarely available. We introduce a decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement with respect to positive-partial-transpose (PPT) states. The regularization of every fixed hierarchy level equals this asymptotic quantity. Additivity at any level therefore yields a single-letter formula, even when the usual one-copy relative entropy is nonadditive. We establish such additivity at the first nontrivial level for two broad multiparameter families, both containing all Werner states. The upper-bound construction also extends to sandwiched Renyi divergences. The hierarchy motivates $k$-multinegative states, a generalization of binegative states and the associated $k$-multinegativity, which gives explicit upper bounds on both the asymptotic relative entropy and exact PPT entanglement cost. We construct states which are $k$-multinegative at arbitrarily large depths $k$ that separate consecutive levels of the previously introduced entanglement-cost hierarchy, disproving its conjectured finite collapse. These results provide state-dependent single-letter formulas while identifying a limitation of universal finite-level characterizations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement with respect to PPT states; each level regularizes to the asymptotic quantity, and additivity at any level yields a single-letter formula. Additivity is proven at the first nontrivial level for two multiparameter families containing all Werner states. Extensions to sandwiched Renyi divergences and a new concept of k-multinegative states are provided, disproving the conjectured finite collapse of the entanglement-cost hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Asymptotic entanglement measures require regularization over infinitely many copies, and single-letter formulas that compute them from one copy are rarely available. The paper aims to make such asymptotic entanglement quantities accessible via computable bounds and to establish when single-letter formulas exist.
AI.method: The authors construct a decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement with respect to PPT states, showing that regularization of each level equals the asymptotic quantity. They prove additivity at the first nontrivial level for two broad multiparameter families. The construction is extended to sandwiched Renyi divergences, and k-multinegative states (generalizing binegative states) are introduced to give explicit upper bounds. States that are k-multinegative at arbitrarily large depths are constructed.
AI.result: Additivity at the first nontrivial level holds for two multiparameter families containing all Werner states, yielding a single-letter formula even when the one-copy relative entropy is nonadditive. k-multinegativity provides explicit upper bounds on both the asymptotic relative entropy and exact PPT entanglement cost. States that are k-multinegative at arbitrarily large depths separate consecutive levels of the entanglement-cost hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: The results provide state-dependent single-letter formulas while identifying a limitation of universal finite-level characterizations, disproving the conjectured finite collapse of the entanglement-cost hierarchy.

title: Proof of a positive coherent-error threshold for topological quantum codes
summary: Threshold analyses of quantum error-correcting codes are well established for stochastic error models, in which errors occur randomly with given probabilities. However, errors in actual devices can also be coherent, such as unwanted $Z$ rotations due to imperfect control, which are not captured by stochastic error models. For the surface code, numerical studies have indicated threshold behavior even under coherent errors, but a rigorous proof of threshold existence is lacking. Here we prove that a positive threshold for coherent $Z$-rotation errors exists for quantum low-density parity-check codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, including the surface code and other topological codes. Specifically, we show that the maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses the entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance up to a prefactor linear in the number of physical qubits whenever the rotation angles lie below a constant that is independent of the code size. The proof combines Fourier analysis to retain the interference among the amplitudes of coherent errors with the cluster expansion of abstract polymer models. Our results expand the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction and offer a statistical-mechanical description of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously proves that a positive threshold for coherent Z-rotation errors exists for quantum LDPC codes with a bounded number of logical qubits (including the surface code), showing that maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance when rotation angles are below a size-independent constant.
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correcting code thresholds are well understood for stochastic error models, but real devices also exhibit coherent errors (e.g., unwanted Z rotations from imperfect control) that stochastic models cannot capture. For the surface code, numerics suggest threshold behavior under coherent errors, yet no rigorous proof of threshold existence existed. This work aims to fill that gap and extend the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.
AI.method: The proof combines Fourier analysis, used to retain the interference among the amplitudes of coherent errors, with the cluster expansion of abstract polymer models. The analysis targets quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, encompassing the surface code and other topological codes, and examines maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery.
AI.result: The authors prove that a positive threshold for coherent Z-rotation errors exists whenever the rotation angles lie below a constant independent of code size. Specifically, maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses the entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance, up to a prefactor linear in the number of physical qubits.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a rigorous threshold for coherent Z-rotation errors in quantum LDPC codes, expanding the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction and providing a statistical-mechanical description of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.

title: Quantum Simulation of Dissipative Non-Markovian Coupled Classical Oscillators
summary: We present a quantum algorithm for simulating classical oscillator networks characterized by non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties, extending recent speedups for undamped harmonic systems to viscoacoustic and viscoelastic media. We embed the history-dependent dynamics into a Markovian state space governed by a non-Hermitian operator by approximating memory kernels through a Prony series. We then use linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation to estimate the instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for a subset of oscillators at time $t$ within error $ε$ using a number of queries to the oscillator system that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(α_{\rm tot} t/ε)$, where $α_{\rm tot}$ is polynomial in the strength of the dissipation, spring constants, inverse masses, and sparsity of the connections in the network. We further show that this energy estimation task is in the worst-case classically hard (i.e., a corresponding decision problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete), even in the presence of strong dissipation. For time-dependent materials, we show that changes in material properties appear as effective dissipation or growth in the energy representation. Additionally, we prove the infeasibility of exponential quantum advantages in locally coupled topologies through a novel form of Lieb-Robinson-like bounds that apply to differential equations. This allows our quantum algorithms to provide quartic speedups for locally coupled damped oscillator systems in three dimensions, raising the possibility of practical quantum speedups for realistically damped oscillator networks and approximated wave equations.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm simulates classical oscillator networks with non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying materials via Prony-series memory kernels in a Markovian non-Hermitian space, achieving query complexity Õ(α_tot·t/ε), proving worst-case classical hardness (BQP-complete) and quartic speedups for locally coupled damped systems in 3D.
AI.motivation: Recent quantum speedups exist for undamped harmonic systems, but realistic oscillator networks feature non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties (viscoacoustic/viscoelastic media), which lack an efficient quantum simulation framework. The paper aims to extend quantum advantages to these practically relevant damped, history-dependent systems.
AI.method: History-dependent dynamics are embedded into a Markovian state space governed by a non-Hermitian operator, approximating memory kernels with a Prony series. Linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) is then used to estimate instantaneous kinetic and potential energy of a subset of oscillators within error ε.
AI.result: Query complexity to the oscillator system scales as Õ(α_tot·t/ε), where α_tot is polynomial in dissipation strength, spring constants, inverse masses, and network sparsity. The energy-estimation task is worst-case classically hard (decision problem is BQP-complete), even under strong dissipation. Time-dependent material changes manifest as effective dissipation/growth in the energy representation. Novel Lieb-Robinson-like bounds for differential equations prove infeasibility of exponential quantum advantages in locally coupled topologies, yielding quartic speedups for locally coupled damped oscillators in three dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The work extends quantum simulation speedups to realistically damped, non-Markovian, time-varying oscillator networks and approximated wave equations, establishing both algorithmic advantages (quartic speedup in 3D local coupling) and fundamental limits (no exponential advantage for local topologies), suggesting practical quantum benefits for viscoacoustic and viscoelastic systems.

title: $k$-fold unbiased measurements and maximal incompatibility
summary: Mutually unbiased bases capture perfect complementarity between two quantum measurements. Extensions beyond pairwise unbiasedness have been proposed, but essentially no non-trivial higher-order constructions are known. We introduce $k$-fold unbiased measurements ($k$-UMs), extending the $k$-fold unbiased bases notion of [arXiv:1706.04446] from rank-one basis measurements to arbitrary-rank projective measurements, and show that this higher-rank setting supports a much richer theory. We develop the notions of algebraic and spectral $k$-UMs and prove that they coincide for rank-one measurements and triples of measurements (3-UMs). We establish strong no-go results for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, but obtain infinitely many higher-rank triples using Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras. We then give these structures an exact operational interpretation in terms of measurement incompatibility. For 3-UMs with any number of outcomes, we determine their generalised incompatibility robustness exactly and construct an explicit joint measurement for their noisy versions at the compatibility threshold. Finally, we implement the symmetry reduction of the sum-of-squares hierarchy recently introduced in [New J. Phys. 28, 064509 (2026)] and give numerical evidence that the noise thresholds arising from the $k$-UM analysis may characterise the asymptotic behaviour of this hierarchy. In particular, with very high precision, we numerically show that our constructed four-outcome 3-UMs are among the most incompatible triples of four-outcome measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces k-fold unbiased measurements (k-UMs), extending k-fold unbiased bases to arbitrary-rank projective measurements, develops algebraic and spectral notions, proves no-go results for rank-one constructions while constructing infinitely many higher-rank triples via Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras, and gives an exact operational interpretation in terms of measurement incompatibility.
AI.motivation: Mutually unbiased bases capture perfect complementarity between two quantum measurements, but although extensions beyond pairwise unbiasedness have been proposed, essentially no non-trivial higher-order constructions are known. The authors aim to fill this gap by generalizing the k-fold unbiased bases notion to arbitrary-rank projective measurements, where a richer theory is expected.
AI.method: They define k-fold unbiased measurements (k-UMs) for arbitrary-rank projective measurements, introduce algebraic and spectral k-UMs, and prove their equivalence for rank-one measurements and triples (3-UMs). They derive no-go results for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, and construct higher-rank triples using Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras. They then give an operational interpretation via measurement incompatibility, computing generalised incompatibility robustness exactly for 3-UMs and constructing explicit joint measurements at the compatibility threshold. Finally, they implement a symmetry reduction of the sum-of-squares hierarchy for numerical analysis.
AI.result: Algebraic and spectral k-UMs coincide for rank-one measurements and 3-UMs. Strong no-go results hold for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, yet infinitely many higher-rank triples are obtained via Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras. For 3-UMs with any number of outcomes, the generalised incompatibility robustness is determined exactly and an explicit joint measurement is constructed at the compatibility threshold. Numerical evidence suggests the noise thresholds from k-UM analysis may characterise the asymptotic behaviour of the sum-of-squares hierarchy, with four-outcome 3-UMs numerically shown to be among the most incompatible triples of four-outcome measurements.
AI.conclusion: Extending unbiasedness to arbitrary-rank projective measurements yields a substantially richer theory than the rank-one setting, enabling infinite higher-rank constructions despite no-go results at rank one. The k-UM framework admits an exact operational interpretation via measurement incompatibility, and its noise thresholds may govern the asymptotic behaviour of the sum-of-squares hierarchy, identifying the constructed four-outcome 3-UMs as near-optimally incompatible.

title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
summary: Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a blind quantum computation protocol based on Pauli-based computation, achieving server resource costs that scale only with the non-Clifford gate count, while retaining fault tolerance and qubit virtualization, and introduces a complementary entanglement-based dual protocol with reduced execution cost.
AI.motivation: Blind quantum computation lets low-resource clients securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but the server's resource costs scale with overall computation size, creating an implementation bottleneck. The work aims to reduce this server-side overhead while preserving security and practical advantages.
AI.method: The authors leverage Pauli-based computation (PBC) to design a BQC protocol in which the server's size depends only on the number of non-Clifford gates. The protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC. They also construct an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation.
AI.result: The protocol yields BQC with server size scaling solely with the non-Clifford gate count. It demonstrates that classical-client BQC is possible even without classical simulability. The entanglement-based dual protocol achieves a dramatically reduced execution cost for resource state computation.
AI.conclusion: PBC enables resource-efficient blind quantum computation with server cost tied to non-Clifford gates, extends feasibility of classical-client BQC beyond classically simulable settings, and offers a lower-cost dual protocol via entanglement, advancing practical BQC implementations.

title: Efficient Non-Uniform Quantum Hermite Transform through Adaptive Sampling
summary: On the span of the first $N$ oscillator modes, Gauss--Hermite quadrature gives an exact change of basis between mode coefficients and $N$ weighted position space samples. We implement this transform with $O(N\operatorname{polylog}(N,1/\varepsilon))$ logical gates and polylogarithmic quantum width. The operator-error bound $\varepsilon$ holds on arbitrary superpositions and includes all auxiliary registers. The construction uses signed averages on adaptive windows to convert uniform-grid samples into weighted Hermite-root samples. Their varying widths control the amplification cost, giving the near-linear bound.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quantum circuit that implements an exact change of basis between the first N oscillator (harmonic oscillator) mode coefficients and N weighted position-space samples, using Gauss-Hermite quadrature. The transform runs in O(N polylog(N, 1/ε)) logical gates with polylogarithmic width, achieving operator-error ε on arbitrary superpositions including auxiliary registers.
AI.motivation: Converting between the occupation-number (mode coefficient) representation and position-space samples is a fundamental primitive for simulating oscillator modes (e.g., bosonic/continuous-variable systems) on quantum computers. An exact, efficient, and error-controlled basis transform grounded in Gauss-Hermite quadrature would enable such simulations, but naive implementations lack near-linear gate cost, low (polylogarithmic) width, and rigorous operator-norm error bounds over all registers.
AI.method: The construction uses Gauss-Hermite quadrature, which exactly relates mode coefficients to N weighted position-space samples. It applies signed averages over adaptive windows to convert uniform-grid samples into samples at the Hermite roots (the quadrature nodes). The varying widths of these windows govern the amplification cost, yielding the near-linear gate bound. The circuit is implemented with O(N polylog(N,1/ε)) logical gates and polylogarithmic quantum width, and the error bound is established in the operator norm over arbitrary superpositions, accounting for all auxiliary registers.
AI.result: The transform is realized with O(N polylog(N, 1/ε)) logical gates and polylogarithmic quantum width. The operator-error ε holds for arbitrary superpositions and includes all auxiliary registers. The adaptive-window signed-averaging technique achieves the near-linear gate complexity via control of amplification cost through window widths.
AI.conclusion: Gauss-Hermite quadrature provides an exact mode-coefficient-to-weighted-position-sample change of basis, which can be implemented as an efficient quantum transform with near-linear gate complexity, polylogarithmic width, and a rigorous operator-error guarantee over all registers, offering a practical primitive for oscillator-mode simulation.

title: Mermin-Peres magic rectangles modulo odd primes
summary: The Mermin-Peres magic square provides a simple example of a system of linear equations over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ which has no classical solutions but does have a finite-dimensional operator solution. For a long time, it was not known how to construct similar examples over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ with $d$ odd. In this paper, we construct, for every integer $d\ge2$, a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ that has a finite-dimensional operator solution but no classical solution. For an odd prime $p$, our operators act on two $p$-dimensional qudits and generate a finite $p$-group obtained by adjoining diagonal polynomial phase operators to the generalized Pauli group. Classical inconsistency follows from an elementary linearity argument comparing assignments on abelian subgroups.

AI.tldr: For every integer $d\ge2$, the authors construct a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ that admits a finite-dimensional operator solution but has no classical solution, generalizing the Mermin-Peres magic square to all moduli, including odd $d$.
AI.motivation: The Mermin-Peres magic square is a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ with no classical solution but with a finite-dimensional operator solution. Constructing analogous examples over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ for odd $d$ had remained an open problem for a long time.
AI.method: For each integer $d\ge2$, the authors build a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$. For odd prime $p$, the operators act on two $p$-dimensional qudits and generate a finite $p$-group formed by adjoining diagonal polynomial phase operators to the generalized Pauli group. Classical inconsistency is established via an elementary linearity argument comparing assignments on abelian subgroups.
AI.result: The construction yields, for every $d\ge2$, a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ that possesses a finite-dimensional operator solution while admitting no classical solution, thereby extending the magic-square phenomenon to odd moduli.
AI.conclusion: The long-standing gap of constructing operator-solvable but classically unsolvable linear systems over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ with odd $d$ is resolved, giving such systems for all integers $d\ge2$.

title: Quantum Entropy Contraction and Factorization from Hypercontractivity
summary: We prove that hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction for a single quantum channel, without a detailed balance condition. For primitive quantum Markov semigroups that are KMS-symmetric with respect to a faithful invariant state \(σ\), we obtain the modified Log-Sobolev bound $α_1\geq \fracλ{(2+\log\|σ^{-1}\|_\infty)}$ where $λ$ is the spectral gap. This removes the assumption of \(L_p\)-regularity for the comparison through the log-Sobolev constant. As an application, we show that the hypercontractivity of an average of two conditional expectations implies the approximate tensorization of relative entropy.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction (modified log-Sobolev) for a single quantum channel, and deduces approximate tensorization of relative entropy for averages of conditional expectations.
AI.motivation: Prior comparisons between hypercontractivity and log-Sobolev/entropy-contraction constants in quantum Markov semigroups typically require extra assumptions, notably a detailed balance condition and L_p-regularity. The paper aims to remove these assumptions.
AI.method: For primitive quantum Markov semigroups that are KMS-symmetric with respect to a faithful invariant state sigma, the authors directly prove an entropy-contraction bound from hypercontractivity, obtaining the modified log-Sobolev estimate alpha_1 >= lambda / (2 + log ||sigma^{-1}||_infty), where lambda is the spectral gap.
AI.result: A modified log-Sobolev bound in terms of the spectral gap is established without a detailed balance assumption or L_p-regularity. As an application, hypercontractivity of an average of two conditional expectations is shown to imply approximate tensorization of relative entropy.
AI.conclusion: Hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction for a single quantum channel; the comparison to modified log-Sobolev constants holds under KMS symmetry alone, and yields approximate tensorization results for averages of conditional expectations.

title: Procrastinating einselection in non-Markovian quantum dynamics
summary: Among the processes governed by open-system and dissipative quantum dynamics, environment-induced superselection, or einselection, is particularly foundational, since it describes the formation of a preferred set of pointer states through environmental monitoring and ultimately the emergence of classicality. Especially in the context of Quantum Darwinism, einselection can be studied in terms of the motion of an observable towards its pointer value. To this end, we derive a quantum speed limit for observables for finite-dimensional systems governed by differentiable time-local open dynamics. We identify two mechanisms through which non-Markovianity can enhance observable speed: direct dissipative motion supported by population retention or revival, and indirect enhancement through restoration of the asymmetry available for coherent motion. For permanent einselection, this delays the emergence of the pointer basis due to accumulated negativity.

AI.tldr: A quantum speed limit for observables under time-local open dynamics is derived, revealing two mechanisms by which non-Markovianity can enhance observable speed, with implications for einselection timescales.
AI.motivation: Einselection—environment-induced superselection—is foundational for explaining classicality, and Quantum Darwinism studies it via an observable's motion toward its pointer value. A quantitative bound on how fast observables can move is needed to understand the timescale of this process, especially under non-Markovian open dynamics.
AI.method: The authors derive a quantum speed limit (QSL) for observables in finite-dimensional systems governed by differentiable time-local open dynamics, then analyze the roles of dissipation and coherence in bounding observable speed.
AI.result: Two mechanisms for non-Markovian enhancement of observable speed are identified: (1) direct dissipative motion supported by population retention or revival, and (2) indirect enhancement via restoration of the asymmetry available for coherent motion.
AI.conclusion: For permanent einselection, non-Markovianity delays the emergence of the pointer basis due to accumulated negativity.

title: Analytic leakage suppression with a single control field: fast two-qubit gates with tunable couplers
summary: Simple analytic pulse-shaping techniques are of great practical utility in quantum control, with prime examples being the DRAG method for suppressing leakage in superconducting microwave gates and the transitionless-driving approach to shortcuts-to-adiabaticity. Standard versions of these methods require two orthogonal control channels, with the second channel effectively breaking time-reversal symmetry. This appears to rule out their use in settings with only a single real-valued control field, such as the kind of baseband flux control that is common in many superconducting circuit architectures. We show here that a simple analytic pulse-shaping technique derived via a Magnus expansion is effective even with just a single baseband control channel. We demonstrate its efficacy by simulating a two-qubit gate between transmons realized with a tunable coupler and baseband flux pulses. Our corrections dramatically reduce non-adiabatic leakage caused by ramping the coupler: for realistic device parameters, leakage in a fast iSWAP gate is suppressed by up to three orders of magnitude. Our approach is general, goes beyond simply suppressing unwanted spectral weight at leakage transitions, and can be applied to a variety of platforms.

AI.tldr: A simple analytic pulse-shaping technique based on a Magnus expansion suppresses non-adiabatic leakage in single-channel baseband flux control, reducing leakage in a fast iSWAP gate by up to three orders of magnitude for realistic transmon/coupler parameters.
AI.motivation: Simple analytic pulse-shaping methods (e.g., DRAG, transitionless driving) are highly practical for quantum control, but their standard forms require two orthogonal control channels that break time-reversal symmetry. This seems to exclude single real-valued control settings, notably the baseband flux control common in many superconducting circuit architectures, leaving a gap for analytic leakage suppression there.
AI.method: The authors derive a simple analytic pulse-shaping technique via a Magnus expansion that operates with only a single baseband control channel. They validate it by simulating a two-qubit gate between transmons implemented with a tunable coupler driven by baseband flux pulses, applying the corrections to suppress non-adiabatic leakage from coupler ramping.
AI.result: For realistic device parameters, the corrections suppress leakage in a fast iSWAP gate by up to three orders of magnitude. The technique goes beyond merely canceling unwanted spectral weight at leakage transitions.
AI.conclusion: A Magnus-expansion-derived analytic pulse-shaping method enables effective leakage suppression even with a single baseband control channel, is general rather than transition-specific, and can be applied to a variety of platforms.

title: All causally separable quantum processes are quantum circuits with classical control of causal order
comment: Upon completion of this work we became aware of arXiv:2609.18559, which proves the same result as ours
summary: The concept of causal (non)separability describes whether the causal order between parties that perform local quantum operations is well-defined or indefinite. Causal (non)separability in the general multipartite setting was introduced and studied in [Oreshkov and Giarmatzi, New J. Phys. 18, 093020 (2016); Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard, New J. Phys. 21, 013027 (2019)]. We resolve an open problem from these earlier works by showing -- using a novel "coherent teleportation technique" -- that a sufficient condition for causal separability identified in [Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard, New J. Phys. 21, 013027 (2019)] is also necessary, and thus provides a complete characterisation of multipartite causal separability. A consequence of this result is that all causally separable processes admit a realisation as generalised quantum circuits in which the order between the operations is classically controlled, known as "quantum circuits with classical control of causal order".

AI.tldr: This work completes the characterisation of multipartite causal separability by proving that a previously identified sufficient condition is also necessary, via a novel coherent teleportation technique.
AI.motivation: Causal (non)separability—whether the causal order between local quantum operations is well-defined or indefinite—was introduced for the multipartite setting in earlier works, but whether the known sufficient condition for causal separability is also necessary remained an open problem.
AI.method: The authors employ a novel "coherent teleportation technique" to establish the necessity (and hence completeness) of the sufficient condition for multipartite causal separability identified by Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard.
AI.result: The previously sufficient condition for causal separability is shown to be necessary as well, yielding a complete characterisation of multipartite causal separability.
AI.conclusion: All causally separable processes can be realised as generalised quantum circuits in which the order between operations is classically controlled—i.e., quantum circuits with classical control of causal order.

title: Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes
summary: We construct explicit families of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits. More precseily, we construct explicit quantum LDPC CSS codes over qubits having constant rate, constant relative distance and constant weight local testers with constant soundness.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs explicit families of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) over qubits, achieving constant rate, constant relative distance, and constant-weight local testers with constant soundness.
AI.motivation: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes—combining constant rate, constant relative distance, and efficient local testability—had been a longstanding open challenge, particularly over qubits. Prior constructions generally fell short on simult10aneously satisfying these parameters, motivating an explicit construction.
AI.method: The authors give an explicit construction of quantum LDPC CSS codes over qubits. These codes admit local testers of constant weight and achieve constant soundness.
AI.result: The construction yields explicit quantum LDPC CSS codes over qubits with constant rate, constant relative distance, and constant-weight local testers with constant soundness, i.e., asymptotically good qLTCs.
AI.conclusion: The work resolves the long-standing goal of explicitly building asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits, demonstrating that all desirable parameters can be achieved simultaneously.

title: Parallel quantum channel discrimination and numerical ranges in tensor product subspaces
summary: Quantum channel discrimination plays a crucial role in quantum information theory. Of particular interest is the case in which the channels can be discriminated perfectly. In this work, we focus on the perfect quantum channel discrimination task in a parallel scheme. We develop an SDP formulation combined with a bisection procedure to compute a quantum state for perfect discrimination in time linear in the number of copies. In addition, we obtain the minimal number of copies of quantum channels to achieve perfect discrimination. Thanks to that, we settle in the affirmative Conjecture 1 of Duan, Guo, Li and Li [arXiv:1605.02294, IEEE ISIT 2016], which characterizes the number of parallel uses needed to discriminate perfectly a distinguished family of operator subspaces. All our results are obtained using the notion and basic properties of the numerical range. In particular, the key fact that we prove and use is that the minimal angle of the numerical range of a tensor product of matrix subspaces equals the sum of the minimal angles of the numerical ranges of the individual subspaces.

AI.tldr: This paper studies perfect quantum channel discrimination in the parallel scheme, providing an SDP-plus-bisection algorithm to construct discriminating states in time linear in the number of copies, determining the minimal number of copies needed, and resolving an open conjecture of Duan, Guo, Li and Li via numerical range techniques.
AI.motivation: Quantum channel discrimination is central to quantum information theory, and the perfect-discrimination regime is especially interesting. Prior work left open the question of how many parallel uses (copies) of the channels are required for perfect discrimination, including a specific conjecture by Duan, Guo, Li and Li on distinguishing a family of operator subspaces.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a semidefinite program (SDP) combined with a bisection procedure, which computes a discriminating quantum state in time linear in the number of copies. They work within the parallel scheme and exploit the notion and basic properties of the numerical range, proving a key fact: the minimal angle of the numerical range of a tensor product of matrix subspaces equals the sum of the minimal angles of the numerical ranges of the individual subspaces.
AI.result: The SDP-plus-bisection approach yields a discriminating state with run time linear in the number of copies, and the minimal number of copies of the quantum channels required for perfect discrimination is obtained. Using the numerical range result, the authors settle in the affirmative Conjecture 1 of Duan, Guo, Li and Li (arXiv:1605.02294, IEEE ISIT 2016), characterizing the number of parallel uses needed to perfectly discriminate a distinguished family of operator subspaces.
AI.conclusion: Perfect quantum channel discrimination in the parallel scheme can be solved efficiently via an SDP formulation with bisection, and the minimal copy number is determined. The additive behavior of minimal numerical-range angles under tensor products is the central tool, enabling an affirmative resolution of the Duan–Guo–Li–Li conjecture.

title: Locally optimized variational evolution for quantum many-body systems
summary: Conventional quantum advantage in many-body dynamics is based on avoiding the simulation cost on a classical computer that arises from the extensive exponential complexity of the global wavefunction. Local observables, however, do not inherit this extensive complexity and may instead be governed by an intrinsic local complexity that is independent of the total system size. This distinction is particularly relevant in thermalising systems, where local observables lose memory of microscopic details and relax towards equilibrium values determined by only a few parameters. Here we introduce a variational time-evolution principle that exploits this distinction by replacing global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The resulting evolution retains coherent short-time dynamics while exploiting the simplification produced by thermalisation at later times. The concrete algorithm we propose is based on locally optimising matrix-product states and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle. We show that the same variational principle has a quantum-classical counterpart, combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with an optimisation strategy robust to both shot and hardware noise. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a variational time-evolution principle that replaces global-state fidelity with a cost function on local reduced density matrices, exploiting the low local complexity of thermalising systems. The algorithm locally optimises matrix-product states with closed-form equations analogous to TDVP, and has a quantum-classical counterpart combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with noise-robust optimisation, demonstrated on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum advantage in many-body dynamics relies on the extensive exponential complexity of the global wavefunction, but local observables do not inherit this extensive complexity. In thermalising systems, local observables relax to equilibrium values governed by only a few parameters, and this intrinsic local complexity is independent of total system size. Existing methods based on global-state fidelity fail to exploit this simplification.
AI.method: The authors introduce a variational time-evolution principle that replaces global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The proposed algorithm is based on locally optimising matrix-product states and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP). The same variational principle has a quantum-classical counterpart, combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with an optimisation strategy robust to both shot and hardware noise.
AI.result: The variation retains coherent short-time dynamics while exploiting the simplification produced by thermalisation at later times. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.
AI.conclusion: By shifting the variational cost from global-state fidelity to local reduced density matrices, the method captures short-time coherent dynamics while benefiting from thermalisation-induced simplification. The approach bridges classical tensor-network methods and quantum hardware implementations, offering a noise-robust route to simulating local many-body dynamics.

title: Environment Alignment and Redundant Record Formation in Imperfect-CNOT Quantum Darwinism
comment: 20 pages including references, 9 figures; plus 10 pages of Supplemental Material with 7 figures
summary: Quantum Darwinism explains objective information through redundant environmental records. Earlier work established that imperfect records can be amplified and that environment self-evolution can enhance or suppress their formation. We investigate how preparation, interaction angle, and field disorder combine in an imperfect-CNOT model with random Gaussian couplings and pure, noninteracting environment qubits. We find that, without fields, a single alignment parameter $Λ$ determines the preparation and interaction-angle dependence of conditional-state distinguishability. Increasing interaction imperfection or local field strength can improve or suppress recording. We explain this nonmonotonic response through the geometry of conditional branch separation. For the pure initial environments considered here, the $Z$ basis remains optimal for Holevo information, so field-assisted recording requires no change of the recorded system observable. Comparing uniform local field strengths with Gaussian-distributed strengths at equal root-mean-square strength shows how disorder broadens both beneficial and detrimental field effects. Exact expressions for fragment information and numerical simulations with up to 24 environment qubits quantify the distinction between high mean information and reliable records across fragments and throughout a finite observation window. These results connect the geometry of local information acquisition to the fragment sizes needed for robust recording. The branch-distinguishability analysis itself requires only the conditional evolution of each environment qubit and extends to other interactions that preserve a system pointer basis.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how preparation, interaction angle, and field disorder shape redundant environmental recording in an imperfect-CNOT model with random Gaussian couplings and pure noninteracting environment qubits, showing a single alignment parameter controls distinguishability and that fields can nonmonotonically help or hinder recording via conditional-branch geometry.
AI.motivation: Quantum Darwinism accounts for objective information via redundant environmental records, but earlier work left unclear how multiple realistic imperfections—preparation, interaction angle, and field disorder—combine to affect record formation in imperfect-CNOT settings with random couplings.
AI.method: The authors use an imperfect-CNOT model with random Gaussian couplings and pure, noninteracting environment qubits. They analyze conditional-state distinguishability, derive exact fragment-information expressions, and run numerical simulations with up to 24 environment qubits, comparing uniform local fields against Gaussian-distributed field strengths at equal root-mean-square strength.
AI.result: Without fields, a single alignment parameter Λ governs the preparation and interaction-angle dependence of conditional-state distinguishability. Increasing interaction imperfection or local field strength can either improve or suppress recording. For pure initial environments, the Z basis remains optimal for Holevo information, so field-assisted recording needs no change of the recorded observable. Disorder broadens both beneficial and detrimental field effects, and exact expressions plus simulations quantify the gap between high mean information and reliable fragment records over a finite observation window.
AI.conclusion: The geometry of local information acquisition links directly to the fragment sizes required for robust recording. The branch-distinguishability analysis relies only on each environment qubit's conditional evolution and extends to other interactions that preserve a system pointer basis.
